articles.headline: 'A huge milestone' - Kartal becomes second Brit ever to reach WTA 1000 final
keyFacts: Sonay Kartal defeated Jelena Ostapenko to reach her first-ever WTA 1000 final at the Wuhan Open.
Kartal became the second British woman to reach a WTA 1000 final and will become the new British No 1.
Kartal will play in the WTA Wuhan Open final on Sunday against either Iga Swiatek or Maja Chwalinska.
body: Sonay Kartal: British star digs deep to beat Jelena Ostapenko and secure a spot in her first-ever WTA 1000 final

Sonay Kartal defeats Jelena Ostapenko to reach her first-ever WTA 1000 final against former world No 1 Iga Swiatek or French Open finalist Maja Chwalinska; You can watch the WTA Wuhan Open final - live on Sky Sports on Sunday from 11.30am
Saturday 17 October 2026 12:59, UK
Britain's Sonay Kartal was forced to dig deep to beat Jelena Ostapenko and secure a spot in her first-ever WTA 1000 final on Saturday.
Kartal became only the second British woman, after Johanna Konta (Beijing 2016, Miami 2017, Rome 2019), to reach a WTA 1000 final with a stunning 7-6 (11-9) 7-6 (7-5) victory over Ostapenko.
Currently 170th in the WTA rankings, Kartal will break inside the top 50 and become the new British No 1 after becoming the lowest-ranked player to reach the final in Wuhan.

The 24-year-old, playing in only her third tournament since returning from a back injury, saved multiple set points to punish Ostapenko, despite the Latvian hitting an astonishing 50 winners in the match.

Kartal, who made her breakthrough by reaching the fourth round of last year's Wimbledon, said: "That was one of the toughest matches I've played.

"I know exactly how she was going to play. At times she's unplayable, but sometimes you have to ride that wave and mentally this is one of the best performances I've had in my career so very proud of that one.

"I was dreaming of playing this match before the injury so to be able to come back here in my third event and to achieve this regardless is a huge milestone for me, so I'm going to recover and enjoy every second tomorrow."
After reaching the fourth round of Indian Wells in March, Kartal missed six months with a stress fracture in her back, returning last month at the Billie Jean King Cup Finals.
Kartal, previously ranked as high as No 44 in the world, reached the third round in Beijing last week.

In Wuhan, she has swept past world No 48 Anhelina Kalinina, world No 12 Belinda Bencic, two-time Grand Slam singles finalist Jasmine Paolini, four-time major semi-finalist Svitolina, and now former French Open champion Ostapenko.
Kartal missed three of this year's four Grand Slams, including Wimbledon.
'Kartal playing the tennis of her life'

Speaking on Sky Sports Tennis, Colin Fleming said: "Her ability to stay in the present got her through. She kept cool to ultimately outlast Ostapenko, who hit 50 winners past her and still couldn't win a set.
"Just a brilliant achievement and the run doesn't stop here. She's playing the tennis of her life and she's got every chance of getting her hands on the title."

articles.headline: How to get Alucard’s Sword and Shield in Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse
keyFacts: Players can obtain Alucard's Sword and Shield in Castlevania: Belmont's Curse by reaching Alucard's Tower in the Main Hall.
Reaching the area requires the Double Jump ability to travel through the Mirror of Life in the Entrance Corridor.
To open the shrine path, players must destroy five blue flames along the path using their Arcane whip.
body: Alucard’s Sword and Shield is one of the best weapons available in Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse, bit it won’t be handed out to you. Instead, you’ll need to unlock the weapon by obtaining it on your adventure.
In this guide, I will help you out by listing its exact location.
How to unlock Alucard’s Sword and Shield in Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse

First, you have to complete the game until you reach Alucard’s Tower in the Main Hall. This is the main location of the weapon. To get the Shield and Sword, we will be heading to the top part of the area, above the library’s entrance.

Screenshot by Destructoid So, how do you reach the tower? First, go to the Entrance Corridor’s Mirror of Life, and use your whip on the painting to reach the nearby glowing red door. You can only get this part done if you have unlocked the Double Jump movement ability.

Screenshot by Destructoid Next, head to the red door in the Grand Hall. There will be challenges along the way, and a part of the path will be created with switches. Keep heading upwards, and you’ll come across an Alucard portrait.

Screenshot by Destructoid When you try to reach the upper level, you’ll find the door blocked by five blue flames. Find them along around the path to the tower, and use your Arcane whip to destroy them all.
Finally, the locked path will be open, allowing you to gain access to the shrine. Interact with it to reach the spot where Alucard’s Sword and Shield can be obtained from the wall.

articles.headline: Everton v Chelsea: Premier League – live
keyFacts: Everton and Chelsea contested a Premier League fixture that featured multiple fouls, confrontations, and yellow cards.
A win would temporarily move either fifth-placed Everton or sixth-placed Chelsea into fourth spot in the Premier League.
The live report stated that Barry would spend time on the touchline for injury treatment before getting involved again.
body: 43 min: Garner and Rogers compete for a 50-50 in the middle of the park. Both slightly out of control. Oof! Both stay down. Quite a few unhappy players surround the referee.

40 min: Palmer wins a corner off Armstrong down the left. Henderson sends it long for Caicedo, to the right of the D, just inside the box. He’s facing away from goal, but nevertheless connects with the volley so sweetly. It cannons off the junction of right-hand post and crossbar, nearly rendering the frame of the goal as splinters. Dust. What a strike! So close to the goal of the season.
39 min: Barry hurt himself in taking that shot, and requires a spot of treatment. Looks like he’ll be fine, but he’ll need to spend some time on the touchline before getting involved again.

37 min: It’s Mykolenko’s turn to chop, seeing off Acheampong down the left and rolling into the middle for Barry, who threads a shot towards the bottom left. But there’s no juice behind it, and it tinkles through to Martinez.

35 min: … so yeah, this game needed a spark, and it got one all right, courtesy of Armstrong. Now everyone’s on the edge, and you wouldn’t put too much money on this ending with the full complement of 22 men.

33 min: Acheampong goes into the book for hanging a leg across Grealish. The free kick leads to a brouhaha, Tarkowski needlessly barging Caicedo to the floor. Henderson takes offence. The pair take a hold of each other’s shirt. Rogers gets involved. And then Tarkowski and Rogers go into the book.

31 min: Pedro and Tarkowski come together in the Everton box. Pedro spins his man; Tarkowski holds his arm. Pedro goes over and wants a penalty. He’s not getting one, though VAR takes a look … and you’ve seen them given.

30 min: The free kick’s worked right to left, Grealish slamming a shot straight into the turf. The ball balloons up then looks like dipping just under the bar. Martinez is forced to tip over, but nothing comes from the corner.

29 min: Tarkowski bursts past Rogers with an elegant chop down the right. Palmer barrels in and puts a stop to his gallop by knocking him over. Palmer is fuming, but lucky not to be booked. Then from the resulting free kick …

27 min: The corner is worked back to Grealish down the left. He curls in for Barry, a perfect cross that should result in a goal. But from six yards, Barry slaps his header straight at Martinez, who makes up for his egregious error by snaffling the ball on his line.

26 min: Rohl shoots from distance. Martinez saves, then holds onto the ball for an age. The referee awards a corner by way of punishment, and Neto is booked for his incredulous reaction. And from the corner …

23 min: Spark! Armstrong slides in hard on Acheampong. The challenge is a bit high, and earns a yellow card. Tarkowski is livid, and gets right up in the referee’s grille, but it was a clear yellow. Mistimed rather than malicious, and though VAR has a look with a view to upgrading the punishment, it’s decided that a booking is fair enough.

21 min: Neto finds a pocket of space down the inside-right channel. He cuts back for Henderson, who attempts to pass into the bottom right from the edge of the box. Blocked. A goal at the Hill Dickinson from a former Liverpool captain would certainly have qualified as spark.
17 min: … no, it’s a complete non-event. Dewsbury-Hall’s delivery easily cleared, Grealish’s ball back into the mixer sailing harmlessly out for a goal kick.
15 min: … so having just said that, Palmer gets Chelsea’s first shot on target. It’s from long range, bouncing harmlessly towards the bottom right. Too easy for Pickford.

14 min:Chelsea have started so many of their other games this season quickly, so Everton will be pleased with this start. The visitors have shown next to nothing in attack, though they have enjoyed 69 percent of possession.
13 min: Dewsbury-Hall shields the ball from Caicedo out on the left flank and draws a foul. Garner takes the free kick, and clumsily hoicks it straight out for a goal kick.
7 min: Pedro has taken a whack in the face and is wandering around with a mouthful of gauze. It’s been a slightly strange start to the game. Hopefully some football will break out soon.

4 min: Grealish makes his presence felt down the left, and a throw is won. Mykolenko launches it long. Acheampong heads clear. Then as Everton try to pin Chelsea back, Grealish and Caicedo get involved in a lightly physical back-and-forth, then yap at each other in the excitable style. The referee comes across to get them to pipe down.

2 min: You’ll have noticed there was no pre-match postbag. No emails, you see. Which makes this existential howl from Evertonian Mary Waltz that’s just dropped so very apposite: “Why does no one seem to want us? Everton seems to be the unwanted step child, trying so hard but rejected by their parents.”
Before the kick-off, everyone takes the knee. It’s the first of two weeks of the Premier League’s No Room For Racism campaign. Challenge it, report it, change it.

It’s time for the theme to Z Cars … and here come the teams. Everton in their royal blue, Chelsea in a new white third strip with red pinstripe and retro lion-crawling-all-over-CFC badge. A nod to the early 1990s Commodore era. We’ll be off in a minute or two!

David Moyes talks to TNT. “If we took a few more chances and we hadn’t conceded last week, we’d have a few more points … but it happens in football … we’ve also come back in games when we’ve been getting beat … sometimes you think you should have more but when you look back on it maybe other times you could be a bit fortunate to get some points … [Vitalii Mykolenko] is the only natural left-back we have in the building at the moment, so great to have him back … [Merlin Rohl] … gives me a little more speed and dynamism … we’re up against a really good Chelsea team, especially in the front line so we might have to use Merlin in different roles as well”

Xabi Alonso speaks to TNT Sports. “We needed a win [against Bournemouth] but this was last week … one is not enough … we need to keep going, doing the right things, repeating and always improving game by game … [Reece James’ injury] makes it more limited but we have enough options … Romeo [Lavia] … [Valentin] Barco … they have played and now we have Mo [Caciedo] back and [Jordan Henderson] so we have more options … but for sure it’s a blow … we will need another big one in this stadium against Everton … tough opponent … they are in a good run so we are expecting a tough challenge.”

Everton are currently in a good humour as well. Should they win this afternoon – and given how they’ve triumphed in this fixture in six of its last nine stagings, losing just the once, that’s very much a live prospect – they’ll move into fourth spot in the Premier League, for a couple of hours at least. Chelsea can do likewise.
Everton make two changes in the wake of their 2-2 draw at Hull City. Merlin Röhl and Vitalii Mykolenko replace Micheal Keane and Brennan Johnson, the latter dropping to the bench.
Chelsea meanwhile make one change to the starting XI sent out to thrash Bournemouth 5-1 last weekend. Jorrel Hato comes into the defence at the expense of Pep Chavarría.

Fifth plays sixth at the Hill Dickinson this lunchtime, in a fixture that isn’t so easy to predict.Chelsea have quickly established an identity under Xabi Alonso as the great entertainers: they’ve scored 15 goals in six matches, with 13 whistling in down the other end. Their last two results – a 3-0 loss at Brentford followed by a 5-1 rout of Bournemouth – illustrate what they’re all about right now. Everton are similarly difficult to pin down, veering between doughty low-scoring shut-out wins (2-0 Palace, 1-0 Ipswich) and rollercoaster 2-2 draws (Manchester United and Hull City, Ainsley Maitland-Niles the centre of attention in both games, for wildly different reasons). The Toffees also remain undefeated, no small feat when you consider the downcast mood around the club at the end of an unsuccessful transfer window.

Throw in the fact that Chelsea don’t particularly like coming to visit the blue half of Merseyside – they’ve lost 2-0 and 3-0 on two of their most recent three visits, the other being a goalless draw – and so while they go into this match as favourites, you wouldn’t exactly risk the farm on it. This could be great fun. Kick-off is at 12.30pm BST. It’s on!

articles.headline: Modern Warfare 4 Campaign Reviews Make It Sound Like It’s Surprisingly Good
keyFacts: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4's single-player campaign launched early today for digital pre-orders, ahead of the game's official October 23 release.
Critics praised the six-hour campaign's gameplay and mission variety as a major improvement over last year's Black Ops 7.
Reviewers are withholding final scored reviews until they can spend more time testing the game's multiplayer modes.
body: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 isn’t technically out until October 23, but the single-player campaign went live today for anyone who pre-ordered the digital version and a small batch of early reviews have already weighed in on what players can expect. The TL;DR is that it sounds like MW4 gets back to the meat and potatoes of what the franchise’s campaigns do best, even if it might not ultimately rank among the best of them.

There are no scored reviews yet because everyone is waiting for more extensive hands-on time with the multiplayer, including DMZ, before making a final assessment. The in-progress reviews and impressions, however, are much better than the reception last year’s Black Ops 7 got at launch. While that surreal, always-online co-op campaign left many critics genuinely perplexed and disappointed, it sounds like MW4‘s six-hour, 16-mission campaign does exactly what you’d expect from a subseries that now spans seven separate games.

PC Gamer lauded it as a single-player COD experience not to be skipped, and one with some stellar levels that harken back to peak moments from earlier in the series, though it also found the story rushed and unsatisfying, especially the bits that included actor Mads Mikkelsen. “This was billed as the conclusion of the Modern Warfare story that started in 2019, but in practice, it’s more like a sprint to be done with it all,” the site’s Morgan Park wrote.

IGN had similar critiques but was also similarly impressed with the overall package, and pointed to a mission resembling “Koreaâs answer to D-Day” as one of the campaign’s large scale highlights. And if you’re “retired” Call of Duty leaker TheGhostOfHope, who correctly predicted Phil Spencer’s eventual departure from Microsoft, well then “This sh*t is f*cking insane man.” Here’s what everyone else is saying so far:

Overall, Modern Warfare 4 wraps up the series with several shocking moments and ends on a high note. The pacing never falters despite the two interwoven storylines and alternating POVs, and the wide variety of missions and locations ensure that the story remains engaging. Modern Warfare 4 is another edge-of-the-seat thrill ride. What distinguishes its campaign from others is a feeling that the devs had more time to think through the experience to create something that can serve as a worthy conclusion for the Modern Warfare series. Because of that, Modern Warfare 4âs campaign ranks as the best weâve seen since Modern Warfare 2019. – S.E. Doster

Modern Warfare 4 made me feel something for the series again. A consistently strong set of missions manages to juggle a bloated cast successfully, saying goodbye to familiar faces while building impressive bonds with new ones. Its expansive behind-enemy-lines mission that borrows most of its ideas from the DMZ mode is a real highlight, as is whenever its blockbuster ambitions are fulfilled and full-throttle battles break out. It may not have quite enough to be considered amongst the very best Call of Duty campaigns, but if itâs to be the end of this particular saga, then at least Modern Warfare is going out on a high note. – Simon Cardy

This is the most fun I’ve had with a Call of Duty campaign in years, lending mostly to its new, non-elite faces. Over half of the 6-hour campaign revolves around a crew of young South Korean marines (plus a few Americans) running out the clock on their compulsory military service when North Korea suddenly invades. The guys themselves are familiar archetypesâa serious guy, an audience insert who doesn’t talk much, an American who fills every silence with a jokeâbut they’re basically charming enough that I cared to remember their names. – Morgan Park

When Modern Warfare 4’s missions hit, I’m reminded why the series’ campaigns remain so important in a genre increasingly measured by online success and hours streamed. It might still be junk food â even if this is a higher quality than limp-burger-like Black Ops 7 or Modern Warfare 3’s attempts â but there are glimpses here of how Infinity Ward’s modern approach to a military thriller can still push further. If only they’d let me off the leash a little. – Jake Tucker

There are parts of the story that feel quite emotional and rewarding, while others, such as Mads Mikkelsenâs role in the game, feel a bit undercooked. For what is set to be Infinity Ward closing the door on the Modern Warfare reboot subseries, for now anyway, I believe they have delivered the goods.Â – GyÅzÅ “FairyEmpire” Baki

I can say that fans of CoDâs singleplayer components should not be disappointed with what Infinity Ward cooked up here. I think it could go down as one of the better options in the series, and definitely one to remember for righting the ship after years of uncertainty and questionable decision-making. And to top it all off, the game is gorgeous on PC, offering the best visuals in the franchise to date, making it all the more enjoyable throughout. – Scott Duwe

Where Modern Warfare 4 shines most is in its gameplay, which shouldn’t shock anyone. Call of Duty always boasts world-class gunplay, and mechanically it’s still the best at what it does. What might be more impressive to me is the flow of the campaign, however. Most campaigns do the whole âjump between multiple parties shtickâ, but MW4 does it with aplomb. The cadence is stellar, with pacing that compliments each chapter. I also love the gameplay variety â rarely did I feel weary of what I was doing. There were slow paced stealth sections, fast moving chase sequences; heck, even a level that had me playing Call of Duty: Frogger Warfare. – David Burdette

articles.headline: When purity politics runs its course: Even the most strident DSA politicians must learn to compromise
keyFacts: Analysts stated that Democratic Socialists of America officials must embrace political compromise to effectively manage city budgets and govern.
Political scientist Daniel Schatz warned that businesses can pressure socialist mayors by withholding investments and relocating, shrinking city tax revenues.
Marketing analyst James Colistra predicted that socialist leaders will shift to moderate policies as public pressure builds to keep their jobs.
body: When members of the Democratic Socialists of America win a local election, they fly into office on the wings of soaring rhetoric. Whether it’s New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani calling for the “warmth of collectivism” or Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson urging her public sector employees “to do big, new things,” the DSA-connected players (like all successful elected officials) know how to play to the base.

However, the realities of running a city and wrestling with economic challenges rarely play along with bumper stickers or slogans gleaned from a political science class. Eventually, speeches and campaign promises face consumer needs, annual budgets, and unemployment numbers.

How do elected leaders of a party that defines itself as hostile to capitalism and the private sector adapt when faced with the needs of their local business communities? Will socialist campaign promises go the way of many political vows when the bills come due?

Daniel Schatz, Ph.D., is a political scientist and former visiting scholar at Harvard, Stanford, and Georgetown. He argues that DSA leaders are still politicians who like to stay in office and maintain power. To do so, even the most strident DSA elected officials must learn and embrace the art of compromise.
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (left) and Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson (right). (Ryan Murphy/AP; Lindsey Wasson/AP)

“The DSA may campaign as though politics is a purity contest, but governing a major city means dealing with budgets, employers, public safety, housing, unions and taxpayers,” Schatz said. “City Hall has a way of curing revolutionary romanticism. A mayor cannot run a city on purity tests. Someone still has to collect the garbage, pay the pension bill, and persuade employers not to leave.”
Schatz foresees a reckoning in any given DSA-run city when rhetoric collides with capital flight, shrinking tax revenues, deteriorating services, and angry middle-class voters.

“A mayor can denounce corporations all day, but it is harder to replace their tax base once they relocate,” he said. “The warmth of collectivism cools rather quickly when the financial district empties and the city budget turns red. We will likely see some DSA leaders creep toward conventional Democratic pragmatism — not because they have suddenly discovered the virtues of markets, but because they want to keep their jobs.”

James Colistra put 20 years into working for Forbes ’s business media and integrated marketing. His experience tells him DSA leaders can delay the need to abandon ideology in favor of compromising by making villains or finding alternative targets their followers can blame.

“Political parties mimic the path many brands take,” Colistra said. “By starting out with controversial statements, they gain traction with their die-hard followers. Once they need to appeal to a larger crowd, they have to start focusing on getting people to work together. They will continue to not allow the leader to be questioned by their loyal following by pinning any problems on others — such as Donald Trump.”
If problems persist and consequences build over time, Colistra insists diversion tactics fail.

“As [DSA leaders] start to fall out of favor with the masses — and while many interest groups are pressuring them to change — they will shift to more moderate talking points,” he said. “They will adjust their message to that of more common-sense policies because it’s better to have that greater reach over pleasing a small group.”

A defining motivation of DSA policies is improving conditions for the underprivileged. After 27 years in law practice, aiding clients with immigration legal services and criminal defense, Donald Leeth believes socialist politicians can better serve their constituents in need by learning to compromise and work within the worlds of business and politics.
“It’s not selling out your cause by agreeing to work within the system’s rules,” Leeth said. “I have come to realize that dogmatism will fail when statutes require otherwise.”
Leeth turns to a possible immigration case to demonstrate.

“There may be instances in law where it may seem best to hold your ground and not negotiate a plea, but — if you choose not to plea out to a crime — then a client can end up being deported immediately after sentencing. Many political factions find themselves in this situation as well when their beliefs become dogmatic. There comes a time when politicians need to cut deals in order to obtain results.”

Political scientist Schatz agrees that, while DSA politicians might sweep into City Hall or the local council on the backs of their fellow party members’ near-religious fervor and unwavering support, successful leaders with ambitions greater than just winning a single election must widen their appeal and attract the support of less single-minded citizens.
“Ordinary voters are less ideological than activists,” he said, invoking President Donald Trump , Democrats’ most widely reviled figure.

“If rents rise, jobs disappear, downtowns deteriorate, or public safety worsens, expect DSA members’ blame to be directed outward to Trump, Wall Street, Republicans, state legislatures, billionaires, the media – anyone but the officials making decisions at City Hall. There is always a convenient villain,“ Schatz said. But average residents will judge their mayor by daily life, not by the sophistication of the excuse, he added.

Though history suggests socialist politicians and businesspeople are always in opposition, it’s possible the former learning to work with the latter would keep DSA leaders in power longer with more success.

“Businesses do not need ideological speeches to pressure DSA politicians,” Schatz explained. “They have a more persuasive language: Investment decisions. A major employer can freeze hiring, delay expansion, relocate functions, or stop investing in a downtown. The effects are immediate: less tax revenue, weaker local businesses, and angry workers asking why their jobs are leaving.”

Businesses can also act through chambers of commerce, file lawsuits, create ballot initiatives, and withhold new investments unless taxes, public safety, and regulation are predictable. Working on all of the above can bring a DSA mayor in line and improve municipal conditions.

“The DSA cannot ‘own the means of production’ in a modern American city,” Schatz said. “Capital, talent, and investment are mobile. A mayor may dislike that reality but cannot repeal it. Once companies start leaving, rhetoric gives way to arithmetic. So, the real question is not whether [DSA politicians] will compromise, but when. Governing requires choices. Activism often demands absolutes. That tension will define the DSA in office.”

From his media and marketing perch, Colistra speaks like a campaign adviser.

“Socialist politicians are still politicians,” he said. “The only uncertainty is whether they learn the limits of ideology early enough to govern competently, or only after voters learned the cost of their ideological experiments.”

articles.headline: Our bodies, our choice, our 60-year mistake
keyFacts: A Cornell University student is filing a lawsuit alleging rape following an encounter involving multiple fraternity brothers.
The local district attorney declined to file charges because the woman previously told police the encounter was consensual.
Commentators are using the Cornell case to debate hookup culture and changing definitions of sexual consent.
body: Ideologies often strain when they come into contact with reality.

The intellectual foundations of the sexual revolution are beginning to crumble after two generations of reifying autonomy, vilifying taboos and tradition, and insisting that consent was the only thing that mattered.

But the ethics of the sexual revolution persist as dogma among the elites running academia and the media , and so our culture is failing to make sense of what seven fraternity brothers and one female classmate did on a drunken, drug-fueled evening two years ago at Cornell University.

The woman involved is filing suit, saying she was raped even though plenty of evidence indicates that what went on that evening was consensual by normal understandings of that word. Her contemporaneous sworn statements to the district attorney and her texts to the boys at the time all indicate that she saw the whole thing — sex with six men, plus alcohol and ketamine — as consensual, and she didn’t regret it in the immediate aftermath.

Most tellingly, Jane Doe wrote in one text message, “Our Bodies, Our Choice,” with the implied conclusion: thus nobody else’s business. She defended her orgy by chanting the mantra of the sexual revolution.
Demonstrators rally during a “Stop Sexual Violence” protest at the Washington Monument, Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026, in Washington. (AP Photo/Jose Luis Magana)
Yet some commentators find it impossible that this could have been consensual.

“Here’s one thing I’m confused about re: the Cornell rape case,” feminist commentator Jill Filipovic commented. “The DA says that the reason his office didn’t bring charges is that Jane Doe told police that what happened was ‘voluntary, conscious, and consensual.’ But like … who is going to the police station to report voluntary, conscious, and consensual group sex? Obviously that’s not what she thought it was.”
You can see the sexual revolution crumbling in this one social media post: If it was consensual, it must be good. This wasn’t good, and so it must be nonconsensual.
The logic is sound. It’s the major premise that is flawed. So to save the premise that consent means good, they need to change the definition of consent.

“The definition of non-consent has similarly expanded,” as the Manhattan Institute’s Christina Buttons put it . “Once understood in terms of force and incapacity, it began to change with the rise of ‘affirmative consent.’ … Today, nonconsent can cover silence , insufficient enthusiasm , any level of intoxication , or feeling pressured , deceived , or influenced to engage in sexual activity.”
The Obama White House claimed that 1 in 5 women is sexually assaulted in college but acknowledged that many “don’t call what happened to them rape.”

The steady shifting of the definition of consent is an attempt to bolster the crumbling foundation of the sexual revolution, which lacks the language to discuss an encounter that was consensual yet harmful.
This category doesn’t exist in the dogma of the sexual revolution, but it obviously exists in reality. It obviously happened at Cornell.

It is denigrating to be treated as an object. Also, sex makes one inherently vulnerable, especially the woman, and so sex outside the context of a loving, committed, exclusive relationship is naturally unnerving.

The pill was supposed to remove most of the vulnerability. Any feelings of regret or shame after a consensual encounter were surely just the fault of nagging old repressive taboos, right? And any connection between sex, commitment, family formation, marriage, and love — those were also mere social constructs. Tear down the social constructs, we were told for two decades, and we’d have true emancipation.

“Everyone needs to grow up cause sexuality and sex is changing, and stuff like this is going to become more common,” Jane Doe wrote in a text message to one of the men involved. “I’m also really open minded tho. I luv you king.”
She is right that the norms and beliefs around sex have always changed, but it turns out the nature of sex hasn’t really changed.

The traditional Western social constructs around sex, it turned out, weren’t mere social constructs. They weren’t structures of oppression or anything. They weren’t religious superstitions. They were reflections of human nature, and that’s not changing.

The old-fashioned ideas about sexuality were offensive to our progressive elite because they posited a fundamental difference between men and women, violating the feminist doctrine of gender symmetry — that any differences between the sexes are culturally conditioned.

Gender symmetry was always absurd, and in sex the inherent differences between men and women are most obvious. The sexual revolution, though, had to deny those differences, and so it created a lie, whereby men’s base sexual proclivities — men freed from the oppression of tradition and religion to pursue their desires — became the governing sexual norm for both sexes.
The result was disaster.

“Consensual hookup culture often feels predatory to women because it is,” conservative writer Emily Jashinsky noted. “It preys on women’s desire for monogamy and coupling and love, which many believe there’s a chance of receiving even after casual sex.”

“Hookup culture,” Jashinsky wrote, “demands that women suppress their natural instincts in order to meet the male demand for no-strings-attached sex. Some women are quite happy to do this, but most women find it unpleasant, or even distressing.”

Jashinsky is right, and this is becoming obvious to everyone whose vision is not clouded by ideology. If you shed the pieties of the sexual revolution, the Cornell situation becomes easy to understand: Ketamine-fueled drunken orgies are bad.
IN DEFENSE OF LEVITTOWN

The students involved all treated one another as objects rather than as humans. The sex was not love-giving — it was pure self-gratification, and thus the participants were debasing not only the others, but themselves.
The problem, it turns out, is not that we were defining “consent” wrong. It’s that we tried to balance something as monumental and important as human sexuality on such an inadequate foundation.

articles.headline: Developer cancels public demo of its upcoming horror drinking game, fearing it will be instantly cloned by AI vibe coders: 'We sincerely apologise for the short notice'
keyFacts: Developer Alliance Arts cancelled the public Steam demo for its horror drinking game Drunken Goddess Reflux.
The developer said it fears AI tools could be used to clone the game's gameplay and presentation before release.
Alliance Arts will host closed online play sessions for a limited number of participants instead of the public demo.
body: The developer of an upcoming horror drinking game has cancelled plans for a public Steam demo in favour of private preview sessions, citing concerns that AI vibe coders might use the demo's content to clone the game.

Drunken Goddess Reflux is a "shot glass Russian roulette" drinking game where players square off against an anime demon girl who loves you but also kind of wants to murder you (which sounds like a standard relationship to me), with the goal of getting your girl-frenemy so blotto that she barfs up her soul. Frankly, it doesn't sound like my cup of tequila, although there is a mechanic where the rules of the game grow weirder and wilder the more alcohol you imbibe—which sounds neat.

Regardless, developer Alliance Arts planned to release a Steam demo on October 19, but in a post on X (via Rock, Paper, Shotgun), the studio explained this is no longer the case. Instead, the studio will host "closed online play sessions for a limited number of participants."

"We sincerely apologize for the short notice," Alliance Arts added, before explaining its reasoning behind the demo's cancellation. Apparently, the demo would have come with "some restrictions on posting and streaming gameplay videos", which Alliance Arts decided it wouldn't be able to properly manage.

On top of this, however, the devs are also worried the demo will be exploited to create AI-coded clones. "We're concerned that the demo's content could be used to quickly imitate or replicate the game's presentation and gameplay with AI or other tools, and that such works could be released before launch."

It isn't clear which of these was Alliance Art' bigger worry, but game developers having their projects vibe-cloned is becoming a more frequent issue. Back in March, a developer shared her game prototype online only to have it cloned within five hours. This isn't the only example either, over on Bluesky, McPixel developer Sos Sosowski shared numerous examples of indie game developers having their works almost instantly copied by AI cloners and released on Steam.

Games being flagrantly copied is not a new problem—the mobile space has struggled with it for years. But the way AI tools have sped up the process is clearly a cause for concern among developers—especially since one of the best ways to improve a game's chance of success in today's crowded market is to share the idea early and build a community around it. As such, unless Valve and other game stores take a firmer stance against outright copycats, we may well see more developers adopt Alliance Arts' approach.
From the creators of Edge: A free weekly videogame industry newsletter, featuring in-depth news, expert analysis and exclusive interviews

Rick has been fascinated by PC gaming since he was seven years old, when he used to sneak into his dad's home office for covert sessions of Doom. He grew up on a diet of similarly unsuitable games, with favourites including Quake, Thief, Half-Life and Deus Ex. Between 2013 and 2022, Rick was games editor of Custom PC magazine and associated website bit-tech.net. But he's always kept one foot in freelance games journalism, writing for publications like Edge, Eurogamer, the Guardian and, naturally, PC Gamer. While he'll play anything that can be controlled with a keyboard and mouse, he has a particular passion for first-person shooters and immersive sims.

articles.headline: Republicans have a huge fundraising advantage. Will it matter?
keyFacts: Republicans have built a large fundraising advantage over Democrats ahead of the midterm elections, New York Times reporter Shane Goldmacher said.
Republican campaign cash could limit Democratic seat gains despite polls predicting a midterm blue wave, Goldmacher stated.
Republicans are spending heavily on advertisements to defend Senate seats in Texas, South Carolina, and Kansas, Goldmacher reported.
body: “Wwhen you talk about how many seats can the Democrats gain, given how unpopular Trump is, the Republican money is seen as a real limiter on Democratic chances,” New York Times reporter Shane Goldmacher told Vox’s America, Actually podcast. | Alex Wong/Getty Images

Polls and pundits alike are widely — if sometimes cautiously — predicting a blue wave in the midterm elections on November 3. But there’s an important caveat to predictions of a Democratic triumph: Republicans have far more cash at their disposal.

President Donald Trump’s super PAC alone had around $400 million on hand earlier this fall, and Elon Musk has personally pumped hundreds of millions into critical races, including $158 million for Texas alone .

Democrats, by contrast, have lagged far behind, especially relative to their performance in past cycles, with the party’s candidates propped up more by small-money donors than deep-pocketed institutional players.

Shane Goldmacher, a national political reporter for the New York Times, has extensively covered the role of money in American electoral politics. He spoke with America, Actually host Astead Herndon about where that money is coming from, how the GOP is spending it, and the effect that it might have on the coming elections.
They also discuss the races that aren’t getting funded — and what current fundraising patterns might tell us about the candidates who could be in the mix in the next presidential campaign cycle.

Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full show, so listen to America, Actually wherever you get your podcasts or watch it on Vox’s YouTube channel .

A couple of weeks ago we asked, “What is the GOP strategy to try to win?” And one of the answers we got is they simply have more dollars than Democrats. Everyone’s talking about this GOP money advantage, but how big is it really, and where is it coming from?

It’s bigger than I’ve basically seen in the last 20 years, and it’s almost entirely coming from big donors. President Trump has a super PAC. It had about $400 million in it at the beginning of September, and there was no Democratic counterpart.

And then the Republican National Committee, which is functionally controlled by Trump, had another $130 million . More than Democrats, because the DNC has literally more debts than cash . That’s a half a billion dollars.
You’re saying this is a historic edge.

In 2024, Kamala Harris outspent Donald Trump significantly in the general election. In 2020, Joe Biden significantly outspent Donald Trump in the general. In 2016, Hillary Clinton . And in the midterms along the way, same story .
This is a switch, and when you talk about how many seats can the Democrats gain, given how unpopular Trump is, the Republican money is seen as a real limiter on Democratic chances.
Do we know anything specific about the people putting in money to the Trump super PAC and the RNC to give them such a lead?

Most of these folks are disclosed. And Trump has been pretty open about raising money from the very moment that he won. He’s been pretty clear that he is in business to help people who are helping him. And so there are big crypto industries that are giving money that are expecting or hoping for favorable regulation from the administration.
So it’s a lot of big businesses. It’s a lot of wealthy Republicans who generally support him anyway, and there are industry groups that see benefit to being in favor.

I will never forget, obviously, the scene from Trump’s second inauguration when he had the Zuckerbergs and the Bezoses and Elon Musk behind him . Is that how I should think about the people funding this donor advantage? Is it tech oligarchs? Is it tech forward?

There’s a lot of tech. I wouldn’t say it’s exclusively [tech]. And Musk, by the way, is like an extra pot of money. Musk, the world’s richest person, is said to be spending at least $200 million . So that’s a bigger chunk. He has given some money directly to the Trump super PAC . He’s given some money to these congressional super PACs .

Is this just quid pro quo? Is this just a group of businesses who think, “Hey, no matter how unpopular this guy is, it is worth investing in him and his party because they’re gonna, regulate or not regulate in a way that’s favorable for us”?
It’s not quite just that. He raised a ton of this money when he was not so unpopular. If you want to say something smart that he did, it was that. Throughout 2025 he was raising all of this money.
And I don’t want to overstate the Republican advantage. A lot of these Democratic candidates are raising a ton of money. James Talarico stands out as maybe the peak example of this.

The Texas Senate race is the most expensive race in the country right now , and Republicans are pouring $200 million to save the nominee there. So a big chunk of that advantage is going to Texas. And the Democrats have put very little money from outside groups into Texas .

Talarico has captured the imagination of these small Democratic donors, and he’s raised tens and tens of millions of dollars . I would be shocked if he doesn’t hit $100 million by the end of the cycle.
You reported that the GOP’s pulling back in North Carolina. What should we take from that in terms of how the GOP sees its own landscape when it comes to the federal races?

Where have Republicans put that money? They put it into South Carolina right next door to protect a seat that was once thought, on the Senate front, to be safe for Republicans. This is the former Lindsey Graham seat that his sister is now running in . And then even more of it has gone to Kansas. This is a state that has not elected a [Democrat] to the Senate for nearly 100 years .

If you’re the Republican Party and you’re pulling money out of a state like North Carolina that hasn’t elected a Democrat since 2008 , and then putting it into a place that hasn’t elected one since 1932, that tells you where the, the bar is moving.
I think the concern for Democrats right now is there might be a wave, but Kansas has a big red wall. It’s hard to beat that kind of institutional advantage for the Republican Party.
Considering how close we are to Election Day, like, what are they actually spending this money on? Is it just more ads? Is it just more mailers?

I was in Pennsylvania this month, and I was trying to watch political ads on YouTube for various races. And I was getting pre-roll of three political ads before I watched the political ad I was trying to watch. So much about our elections is being decided now by people who are actively trying not to consume political news. It costs more money to reach people who are avoiding it on purpose.
There are some organizing things that happen, but most of the money is various versions of advertising.
On the Democratic side, considering this GOP edge, what are the races that you currently describe as underfunded? Where do the Democrats wish they had more money?
Number one is governors’ races, actually. When you look at where Democratic donors swoon, it’s Senate races. There are no candidates for governor who have made people swoon like this in recent years.

[James] Talarico is raising all this money, but in Texas also, Gina Hinojosa, the Democratic candidate for governor, does not have that kind of money, and she’s running against Greg Abbott, who had $100 million .
What should we ascribe that to?

I think there’s actually a pretty simple answer, which is, if you don’t live in the state, it doesn’t impact you. If you’re a small donor and you live in California, you can be excited about a Senate candidate because you want Democrats to control the Senate. Are you as excited about a Democratic governor of Georgia?
It’s hard to argue that the governors of these key presidential battlegrounds aren’t some of the most important races on the ballot this year.

By the way, a problem with both parties. Republican national donors and these super PACs also don’t fund these governor’s races at the same level. So it’s not just a Democratic issue, but it’s more acute [for them] because Democrats are so well-funded at the small-donor level.

Fundraising is a huge part of what sets the presidential candidates apart from one another. The money game among those candidates has already started. Is there anyone who’s quietly built some donor network that’s worth thinking about? Is there someone who stood out as a particularly effective fundraiser when we think about the 2028 crowd?

Let me give you my favorite stat from the last Democratic primary, which is that Mike Bloomberg spent twice as much as Tom Steyer, who spent twice as much as Bernie Sanders, who spent twice as much as Joe Biden, who became the Democratic nominee. And so money isn’t gonna determine who wins the next Democratic presidential primary.

One person who has unlimited money, functionally, is JB Pritzker. He’s a billionaire, the governor of Illinois, and he is spending his money now to help other Democrats , which is a good way to make friends.
My last question is an open one. What’s an underexplored story that we should be following going forward when it comes to campaign cash or both parties’ relationship with money?

One of my big questions is what happens to Republican small-dollar fundraising in that post-Trump era. Because there have basically not been any other Republicans who have excited donors for a decade.
Not JD Vance?

I have not seen evidence. JD Vance was not a good fundraiser before he [joined] the ticket with Donald Trump. When he ran for Senate, his primary run was funded chiefly by Peter Thiel through a super PAC.

There are candidates who’ve raised some money, but nothing on the scale of what these Democratic candidates have been able to raise online. When you talk about that Trump era [ending] at some point, are there others who are going to get Republican small donors excited? We don’t know. We haven’t seen it yet.

articles.headline: Grand Theft Auto 4 Was Rockstar at Its Best: Unpredictable
keyFacts: Grand Theft Auto 4 defied series conventions by following Niko Bellic through a smaller, dense version of Liberty City.
The article states GTA 4 provided a mature satire of the American Dream because Niko could not escape criminality.
The author hopes upcoming Grand Theft Auto 6 protagonists will grapple with the consequences of their actions.
body: By the time Grand Theft Auto 4 launched in 2008, Rockstar had carved itself an unassailable niche and a reputation for innovation. And yet for all that praise, it was pretty easy to guess what a new GTA game would be like. The formula changed little from the time the series went 3D. Some vaguely sympathetic character would encounter hardship and then embrace a life of crime as a little treat. That life might look different from game to game, but the general idea remained the same. GTA 4 defied that pattern, and it's one of the reasons it's still an excellent game.

GTA 4 follows Niko Bellic, a former soldier traveling to America both for a better life and to find the man who betrayed his unit in the past. One of GTA 4's biggest surprises at the time was how small Rockstar made this version of Liberty City, a barely disguised post-September 11 New York City. (One of the plot reasons why you can't explore further is that the bridges are up following terrorist threats.) Where the settings of previous mainline games kept getting bigger, Liberty City was comparatively small. And yet it felt more alive than Vice City and Los Santos. It's dank and dark, a pretty miserable place really, and yet captivating and unique. That's by design, and not just the level of verticality and sense of scale Rockstar managed to squeeze into the geographically small(ish) space. Rockstar co-founder Dan Houser said at the time he wanted no dead space in Liberty City. Everywhere had to feel important.

But it's also an example of Rockstar treating a GTA setting with more thought and care. Liberty City seems alive, yes, but it's living the kind of life that mirrors its protagonist. Nico, like countless others in real life, came here expecting a better and brighter future. What he got was embroiled in the city's criminal underworld. No matter his good intentions — no matter what he should've received after a life of service — he just ends up dragged through the mud and forced to set his own wants and ethics aside to get by.

It's one of Rockstar's most mature attempts at satirizing the American Dream (at least in GTA) and it's a marked step up from how previous games treated its characters. Sure, you feel sorry for C.J. in San Andreas after what happened to his mom. And Tommy's friends did him dirty in GTA Vice City. But there's not much more emotional depth here or in most other GTA games. It's hard to see these characters' trajectories and feel sympathetic, when the outcomes (becoming a crime lord, invariably) are so exaggerated compared to the event that pushed them down this path.

Nico's story has no happy ending. Sure, he comes out on top and his place in Liberty City's underworld is secured. This isn't the life he wanted, though, and no amount of glitz and glamor can make up for what he's lost. That's not the ending you expect from a modern GTA. With GTA 6, it looks like Rockstar is leaning heavily into the lovable rogue setup. There's not a lot of room for introspection in that kind of story, but I hope Jason and Lucia at least have to grapple with the consequences of their actions like Niko does.

articles.headline: Apple’s HomeView is just the latest threat to online recipe writers
keyFacts: Apple revealed the HomeView smart display, which converts online recipes into hands-free, step-by-step cooking instructions.
Food writers say stripping recipes threatens their earnings by removing ads, affiliate links, and helpful context.
Creators are increasingly moving to paywalled newsletters, while Apple has not clarified how HomeView handles paywalls.
body: When Apple revealed the HomeView to the world, it did so with an unusual ad for the company: Instead of pristine, polished tech in immaculate rooms, it’s a three-minute look at the messy, frantic morning routine of a family of five. Apple’s new smart display sits in the center of the chaos on the kitchen table, helping the family check their calendars, send messages, and pull up a French toast recipe in seconds, with simple, step-by-step instructions.
Apple’s HomeView is just the latest threat to online recipe writers
Its simplified, hands-free instructions strip out much of what’s essential to online recipes.

The HomeView is just the latest in a long line of websites, browser extensions, and smart home gadgets with the same promise: that it can take an online recipe and strip it down to the essentials. Instead of scrolling a lengthy webpage that might range from helpful cooking instructions to seemingly irrelevant personal anecdotes, with the recipe itself way down at the bottom, you simply get ingredient lists, cooking instructions, and timers, all navigable hands-free with voice controls and Siri AI. No distractions, no unnecessary text, and no need to deal with a touchscreen while you’re wrist-deep in a chicken carcass. The appeal is obvious.

There’s only one group of people likely to object: the food writers who created those recipes in the first place. I would know, since I’m one of them — I have my own food newsletter where I occasionally publish recipes, so I have a little skin in the game. The problem is that converting a recipe into easy-to-follow instructions in Apple’s own format also strips it of its context, including the ads and affiliate links that many recipe writers rely on for their income. Recipes may often be free to read, but they’re not free to create, and solutions like Apple’s remove the main ways websites and writers recoup those costs. “Tools that just extract the recipe,” Eater senior reporter Bettina Makalintal says, “break apart that unspoken social contract with recipe developers and audiences.”

The online recipe landscape is a diverse place. Behemoths like Allrecipes and NYT Cooking host tens of thousands of recipes each, some from professional chefs and others from home cooks. Countless dedicated food publications run original recipe content, and thousands of independent chefs produce their own, across blogs, newsletters, YouTube accounts, and TikTok pages. While much of the writing on a recipe page may get on budding cooks’ nerves — we’ve all heard the jokes about being forced to read someone’s grandma’s life story before getting to their cookie recipe — it’s there for a reason. For one thing, it’s usually the only part of a recipe that a writer can copyright — the rest is regarded as mere instructions. But that extra writing is also there because before it worked so hard to strip the text out, Big Tech insisted on it. “Recipe writers needed to pad out the text in a certain way so that their recipes would have a chance of coming up in a Google search,” Makalintal explains.

The good news for recipe writers is that Apple’s approach guarantees at least one visit to their original web page. To load a recipe onto the HomeView screen you have to first open it either on your iPhone or through Safari on the HomeView itself, ensuring you’ll see its ads at least once. That’s welcome, but for website owners it’s still a lot less valuable than the repeated ad impressions that come from someone scrolling down the page and staying on it while they cook.
“Nearly every food blog has a ‘jump to recipe’ button right up at the top, so you don’t actually have to scroll. So if you’re still out here complaining about these essays, you’re just an asshole.”
— Jaya Saxena

It’s not just bad for the writers, either — readers and home cooks may be missing out too. “The additional information around recipes can sometimes be really helpful when it comes to troubleshooting problems that could come up while cooking or addressing things like ingredient swaps,” says Makalintal. Apple’s simplified steps may make some recipes easier to follow, but others might become harder without crucial context included elsewhere on the page.

And as common as gripes about recipe intros are, they’ve long been easy to skip if you really insist. “Nearly every food blog has a ‘jump to recipe’ button right up at the top, so you don’t actually have to scroll,” says Jaya Saxena, one of the founder-owners of the food website Ravenous. “So if you’re still out here complaining about these essays, you’re just an asshole.”

Apple is far from the first company to attempt to streamline online recipes. In 2021 startup Recipeasly promised to “fix” online recipes by removing the ads and “life stories.” It barely lasted a weekend before online backlash forced its founders to take it offline. Bigger tech companies have been able to plow through that resistance. Amazon’s Echo Show displays offer similar hands-free cooking features to the HomeView’s, though only with partner sites like Allrecipes or Epicurious. Google’s Nest Hubs used to as well, though Google ultimately removed the step-by-step recipe feature from its Nest Hubs in 2024, along with other “underutilized” features. Apple’s approach, which it says will work with any online recipe that uses Google’s search-friendly recipe formatting, is unique among the current smart home hubs. Perhaps most egregious of all, Google Search now uses Gemini AI to amalgamate online recipes, presenting a streamlined version right on the search page, saving users from ever needing to click through to the original sources at all.

Saxena says that for established writers, this is “more like a continuation of the threats they’ve already seen.” Unless Apple sells vast quantities of HomeView displays, its recipe function is still likely to be used by far fewer people than Google’s AI search recipes, let alone recipes from other AI assistants and tools, which are also more egregious in how they take advantage of online content. “I would put the threat level below AI summaries,” says Makalintal, because their “opaque” sourcing “really is erasing labor.”

Some major recipe platforms might be able to reduce the impact by getting on board. While the HomeView doesn’t have its own app store, it does support casting apps to the screen using the same tech as CarPlay. That means big apps like Allrecipes or NYT Cooking will have the option of presenting content on the HomeView on their own terms. Independent writers are unlikely to be able to do the same. For them, the choice remains as it has for some time: Stick it out with ever-diminishing Google traffic and ad revenue; take on more sponsored content and paid-for recipes with big brands; or move to a paywall or newsletter business model.

Smaller recipe developers are turning to Substack, says Makalintal, where it’s easy to lock recipes behind a paywall. I’m one of them — on my newsletter I restrict my recipes to paid subscribers, a reflection of the fact that they’re the most time-consuming articles I publish. I’ve asked Apple how the HomeView recipe tool will handle paywalled recipes, but at the time of publishing haven’t gotten an answer. But the move en masse to newsletter platforms “has led to some subscription fatigue among home cooks,” Makalintal says, and few cooks will start a paid subscription to access a single recipe, suggesting it’s not likely to support the whole industry.

Some version of paid-for content may be the only answer going forward, though, for creators both big and small. Tech companies like Apple will have to grapple with how their tools work when access to free content gets trickier, and the rest of us may have to get used to paying for recipes again.

“A good, creative recipe that has been tested to ensure it really works takes time and effort and money,” Saxena says. “It is a real skill to communicate how something is made when you’re not physically with that person, and buying all the ingredients needed to test things multiple times is expensive. People should probably be more comfortable paying for that.”

articles.headline: Yes, You’re Probably Paying More for Phone Service. Here’s Where Your Money Is Going
keyFacts: T-Mobile, AT&T, and Verizon have raised fees and legacy plan prices, increasing overall costs for mobile phone customers.
These fee hikes bypass multi-year price guarantees because those protections apply only to base plans rather than added fees.
Customers can lower their monthly expenses by switching to prepaid carriers, downgrading service tiers, or utilizing free network trials.
body: Everything is getting more expensive bit by bit, and it’s not just gas or grocery prices. T-Mobile just increased the price of a pair of fees that get added on top of what customers pay for their mobile phone plans, and it’s not the only carrier doing this.
Over the past year and a half, the big three US cellular providers have raised prices in small ways that may not seem consequential month to month, but add up over the year.
More costly fees, taxes and plans

For a while, a lot of carriers’ plans rolled taxes and fees into them as a competitive advantage — when you know you’re paying a fixed amount each month, it’s easier to budget. Unfortunately, those days are over, at least among the big three US carriers: AT&T, T-Mobile and Verizon.
More from CNET

The new fee increases are so small that you probably won’t notice them on your bill. Effective Oct. 12, T-Mobile’s Regulatory Programs and Telco Recovery fees increased for every line on a customer’s account. For voice lines, it’s an increase of $1.00 for the combined fees (previously $4.49 a month, now $5.49 a month). Mobile internet lines, such as those for smartwatches or tablets, went up $0.50, from $2.10 to $2.60 a month.

T-Mobile previously raised the cost of these fees in April 2025, from $3.49 to $3.99 and $1.40 to $1.60, so in a year and a half, customers are paying $2 more per voice line and $1 more per mobile internet line per month.

Even if your plan has a multi-year price guarantee, that applies to the main plan itself, not miscellaneous taxes and fees that are added on top of the plan’s cost. Carriers can, and do, increase those fairly regularly.
For Roger Entner, analyst and founder of Recon Analytics, the problem isn’t that carriers regularly raise fees like this. It’s that they spread out the increases.

“I don’t understand why they [don’t] only piss you off once a year, but instead sometimes choose to piss you off four times a year,” Entner said in a conversation with CNET. “It doesn’t make sense unless you want to be hated.”

T-Mobile isn’t the only one that’s increased these fees. AT&T raised its Administrative and Regulatory Cost Recovery Fee from $3.99 to $4.99 per line in August; that was after a December 2025 increase from $3.49. Verizon raised its fees in August 2025, from $3.50 to $3.78 per month for voice lines and from $1.60 to $3.97 per month for data-only lines.

As for the prices of the plans themselves, they’ve been relatively consistent. The exception is Verizon, which announced holiday deals in December 2025 and carried the pricing all the way through August when it announced the Simplicity plan. The myPlan plans, which include Unlimited Welcome, Unlimited Plus and Unlimited Ultimate, now cost $10 more per line for new customers than they did at the beginning of 2026.

Are these costs enough to inspire customers to look elsewhere? “We’ve done research on what makes people [switch carriers],” Entner said. “Five dollars and below doesn’t matter. People shrug it off. … Where the outrage [would be] is if your price would go up by $15, $20, and nobody’s doing that.”
Retiring legacy plans

When AT&T revamped its unlimited phone plan lineup in March this year. It also announced that prices would be increasing for many of its “retired” plans, as much as $20 for an account (not per line). Then, in August, the increases were applied to more legacy plans, which included the ones that the new 2.0 plans had just replaced a few months earlier.

At the time, an AT&T spokesperson said, “This increase reflects the real cost of continuing to deliver the speed, reliability and support our customers expect every day.” I think it’s also safe to say that this type of increase can also serve as an incentive for customers to migrate to current plans.

In June, however, T-Mobile announced it would unilaterally move some customers to new plans in order to get their old ones off the books. Although T-Mobile said that most plans would be comparably priced to what the customers were paying before, in some cases it meant increases of up to $6 per line per month.
The new plans were variations of T-Mobile’s existing lineup, such as Experience More with Appreciation Savings versus the straight-up increase that switching to the Experience More plan entails.
The move wasn’t optional, and at least one customer filed an informal complaint with the FCC. That’s one step below a formal complaint, which would involve fees and lawyers.
Price guarantees have almost evaporated

In April of last year, Verizon made a big deal about offering a three-year price guarantee on all of its plans. However, the guarantee slipped away in August when the company introduced its Simplicity plan. T-Mobile one-upped Verizon with a five-year price guarantee on its plans, which is now available only on the Experience Beyond 2.0 and Experience More 2.0 plans.
The people who signed up for plans under those terms still enjoy the price protection, but customers looking to jump to a new carrier won’t necessarily get the same deal now.
For existing customers, price guarantees can also act like handcuffs. If they want to move to another Verizon plan, for example, they’ll have to give up that price stability.
Looking at the bigger picture, though, wireless service has gotten cheaper

When I was researching for this article, I came across one written by Entner for LightReading that takes a longer-term view of wireless pricing. It highlights that we’re actually paying less for phone service now than we used to. In “Inflation mostly skipped the wireless bill,” Entner uses industry and government data to show that wireless service has gotten cheaper in real terms since 2007 (the year the iPhone was released).

“The dollars that you spend, yes, it’s going up,” Entner said in our conversation. “When we calculate it as part of your wallet share, [the] percentage of your monthly disposable income, it goes down.”
How can you save money on your phone bill?

A couple bucks in fees here and there doesn’t sound like a lot, but if you have four lines on an account, for example, that’s an extra $8 per month you weren’t paying before. And for people looking for the most economical plan, it’s a larger percentage of their phone bills.
So what options are there to offset the increases or reduce your monthly expense?

One option is to shop around for a prepaid plan. Companies such as Cricket, Mint Mobile and Visible run on the carrier’s networks and can cost less, especially if you’re currently paying for perks such as streaming services or hotspot data you’re not using. (Those three are all actually owned by the big three: Cricket is AT&T, Mint Mobile is T-Mobile and Visible is Verizon). Another option is US Mobile, which lets you choose whichever network is strongest in your area.

A single line on T-Mobile’s Essential Saver 2.0 plan, for example, costs $50 and includes 50GB of high-speed data. Mint Mobile’s 12-month Unlimited plan works out to $30 a month when you prepay $360 for the entire term, and it also includes high-speed data that may be slowed after you use 50GB. It includes up to 20GB of mobile hotspot usage, too.
Although it’s a bigger one-time lift, prepaying for an entire year for a plan like this means you won’t have to wonder how much next month’s bill will be.
You may not be in a position to switch providers, particularly if you’ve financed a phone from your current carrier. But you may be able to drop back to a less expensive plan with fewer features.

Verizon’s Simplicity plan at $45 a month, for example, is $20 less expensive than its Unlimited Welcome myPlan for a single line. (Verizon touts the $30 a month price, but that’s just for new customers who bring their own phone with them.) And Simplicity actually gives you better performance, because you can connect using the faster 5G Ultra Wideband (or 5GUW) if your phone has the hardware for it; Unlimited Welcome is limited to regular 5G speeds.

But Simplicity has an important catch: If you have a multi-line Verizon plan and one person switches to Simplicity, every other line must also switch to it. For a family of four, that means paying $180 a month (at the $45 rate), which is $10 more expensive than the Unlimited Plus myPlan and includes less high-speed mobile hotspot data.

As another example, AT&T’s modular Build-A-Plan costs as little as $15 a month when you bring your own unlocked AT&T-compatible and eSIM-capable phone. That gives you just 1GB of data — and that’s it, but you can add more data and hotspot capability for additional costs.

Then there’s the free option. If you don’t mind ads and the restriction of using a single app for all your communications, TextNow gives you calling, texting and data for email, maps, ride-sharing and finance apps. Unlimited data and calling plans can be purchased for the day ($3), week ($9) or month ($36).

If you’re thinking of switching providers, don’t forget that each one has limited programs to let you test out the speed and coverage in your area. T-Mobile offers a free three-month Network Pass, Verizon has a 30-day “trial” program and AT&T has its own 30-day eSIM free trial program.

It’s never fun to find the bill for your wireless phone service — an expense that feels like a modern necessity — is going up. But there are plenty of alternative options that can save you money, if you know where to look.
