articles.headline: Trump waives several Russia sanctions as row with Zelensky intensifies
keyFacts: Donald Trump waived several congressional sanctions against Russia, stating in an executive order that the suspension was in the US national interest.
President Volodymyr Zelensky and US lawmakers criticized the decision amid escalating diplomatic tensions between Washington and Kyiv.
Ukrainian and US negotiating teams could meet next week following discussions on Friday, President Zelensky said.
body: - Published
Donald Trump has blocked numerous sanctions on Russia two days before they were due to take effect, as a row with his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky deepens.
The sanctions were passed by the US Congress and signed into law by Trump in September.

But the US president issued an executive order on Friday night saying that suspending some was in the US "national interest", prompting a backlash from US lawmakers. Zelensky said it was unfortunate the US has decided to "completely disregard" the sanctions.
Relations between Washington and Kyiv frayed after the US struck a controversial deal to import Russian diesel. Ukraine then accused the Trump administration of withdrawing key military support.

Trump and Zelensky have exchanged sharp words about one another. Ukraine's president declared it was nice to be among "real leaders" while addressing an EU summit, after Trump said Zelensky was "more difficult to deal with" than Russian President Vladimir Putin.

The new US sanctions law took aim at Russia's economy, giving Trump broad powers to levy tariffs of up to 100% on imports from the top five purchasers of Russian oil and gas â most significantly China and India.

It also included sanctions against senior Russian figures, including Putin, as well as Russian financial institutions and Moscow's so-called "shadow fleet" of vessels used to circumvent existing embargoes.
Many of these provisions have now been waived by Trump.
Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev called the waiver "an important and truly historic moment".
Posting on X, he said the sanctions would have inflicted "serious damage" primarily on the US and global market, and that economic cooperation benefits both nations.
Democrats including the Virginia Congressman Don Beyer have criticised the move, accusing Trump of capitulating to Moscow and turning his back on Kyiv and Zelensky.

"Trump's latest surrender to Putin again betrays our Ukrainian partners and defies clear congressional intent of legislation designed to punish Russia for its illegal war of aggression," Beyer wrote on X.
The move is likely to draw further anger from Ukraine, where Zelensky has long stressed the need for stringent sanctions to limit funding Russia can use in its war effort.
Zelensky said on Saturday morning that the sanctions "could have helped enormously" and that the law was "supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia to bring this war to an end".

He pointed to Russian overnight attacks on 15 Ukrainian energy facilities that had caused power cuts in several regions and said: "Russia is trying to cause a blackout in Ukraine â right before winter."
Zelensky said was "important that everyone in America also sees what is really happening" on the ground.
He later told reporters that he believed the Trump administration would lift more sanctions against Russia.
He also said negotiators Ukrainian spoke to their US counterparts on Friday and that both teams could meet next week.

Trump was initially criticised by Zelensky and Ukraine's European allies for temporarily suspending some US sanctions to import Russian diesel in a bid to bring down US energy prices, which have skyrocketed during the Iran war.

Trump has spent months grappling with the political consequences of the Middle East conflict, which has sent fuel costs soaring ahead of the US midterm elections. Rising inflation has soured Trump's standing with the American public.
Zelensky suggested the deal was tantamount to the US investing in Russia's war effort.
A few days later, Trump claimed that both Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an "energy ceasefire" to facilitate the export of Russian diesel.

Both nations have been intensively striking one another's energy infrastructure. Kyiv says this is to limit revenue for Russia's war machine, while Moscow claims it only targets facilities used by the Ukrainian military.

Zelensky initially expressed surprise at Trump's announcement, and said Kyiv would stop the strikes if Russia did the same. After three days which saw several fresh attacks from Russia, Kyiv resumed its strikes on Russian oil refineries.
This prompted scathing condemnation from Trump, who called the strikes a "disgrace". Zelensky replied that he was "only standing up for Ukraine's interests".
Concerns that Trump is siding with Russia have been heightened by disruption to a US-provided satellite system used by Ukraine.

Last week Starlink suddenly and unexpectedly restricted the speed at which drones could fly while still maintaining internet connection. This disrupted some battlefield missions, Ukraine said, and hampered Kyiv's ability to protect itself from incoming Russian attacks.
During the slowdown, Russia launched several deadly strikes on Ukraine, with residents and the government saying these came with no prior warning.
Zelensky said on Friday that Starlink speeds had still not been fully restored.
Trump has denied halting intelligence-sharing and deliberately slowing down Ukraine's Starlink network.
Ukrainian authorities have confirmed that at least nine people have been killed and around 60 injured in Russian strikes across the country over the past 24 hours.
They said an ambulance driver was killed and 20 others were injured in Russian strikes on the city of Kherson on Saturday morning.
Russia's defence ministry said it had targeted industries linked to Ukraine's defence industry - including steel works, an electrical sub-station and a cargo vessel in the Black Sea.
Additional reporting by Helen Sullivan

articles.headline: Indiana, Ohio State make college football history in massive Big Ten showdown
keyFacts: No. 5 Indiana hosts No. 4 Ohio State on Saturday in Memorial Stadium's first matchup between two top-five ranked teams.
Indiana enters the contest with a 22-game winning streak, the longest active streak in the Football Bowl Subdivision.
The game is scheduled for noon ET on Fox, with conference championship and College Football Playoff implications at stake.
body: For decades, Indiana football fans watched Ohio State dominate the Big Ten while the Hoosiers struggled to establish themselves among the conference's elite programs. That narrative has changed dramatically, and Saturday's showdown in Bloomington provides perhaps the clearest evidence yet of just how far Indiana has come. The No. 5 Hoosiers will host No. 4 Ohio State on October 17 in what could become the biggest home game in Indiana football history.

The matchup marks the first time Memorial Stadium has hosted a game between two teams ranked inside the nation's top five. It also brings together the winners of the last two national championships, with Ohio State capturing the 2024 title and Indiana completing its remarkable championship run in 2025. Both teams enter undefeated in Big Ten play, adding significant conference championship and College Football Playoff implications to an already fascinating rivalry.

Indiana brings a 6-0 record and the nation's longest active winning streak into the contest, while Ohio State arrives at 5-1 with an opportunity to avenge its loss in last season's Big Ten Championship Game. Kickoff is scheduled for noon ET on Fox, with Gus Johnson, Joel Klatt and Jenny Taft on the broadcast.
Indiana's remarkable winning streak has college football's attention

Curt Cignetti has accomplished something that would have seemed almost impossible to Indiana football fans just a few years ago. The Hoosiers have won 22 consecutive games, the longest active streak in the Football Bowl Subdivision. Indiana has also won 19 straight home games and has never lost at Memorial Stadium under Cignetti, who has transformed the program into a legitimate national championship contender.

The numbers become even more impressive when considering Indiana's history. The Hoosiers entered Cignetti's tenure with more all-time losses than any other major college football program. Now, they have won 33 games since the beginning of the 2024 season, the most successful three-year stretch in school history. Indiana has started 6-0 in each of Cignetti's first three seasons, establishing a level of consistency that previous generations of Hoosiers fans could only imagine.

Saturday presents another opportunity to extend that success. A victory would give Indiana 23 consecutive wins, matching Ohio State's streak from the 2013 and 2014 seasons. It would also extend the Hoosiers' remarkable home winning streak against one of the most talented opponents on their schedule.

The historical significance is difficult to overstate. Ohio State leads the all-time series 81-13-5, and before Indiana's victory in the 2025 Big Ten Championship Game, the Hoosiers had not defeated the Buckeyes since 1988. Indiana's 13-10 championship victory last December ended decades of frustration and demonstrated that the program could compete with college football's traditional powers.
Josh Hoover gives Indiana another dangerous quarterback

One of the biggest questions surrounding Indiana entering the season was how the Hoosiers would replace Fernando Mendoza, the quarterback who helped lead the program to its national championship. Josh Hoover has provided an impressive answer, delivering efficient production while protecting the football at an extraordinary level.

Hoover enters Saturday having completed 68.2 percent of his passes for 1,364 yards, 17 touchdowns and no interceptions. He is one of only two quarterbacks nationally with at least 15 touchdown passes and zero interceptions this season, joining Miami's Darian Mensah. His ability to make accurate throws without giving opponents additional possessions has become a defining part of Indiana's offense.

The former TCU quarterback also demonstrated his ability to perform under pressure during last weekend's dramatic 20-17 victory at Nebraska. Indiana trailed 17-6 in the fourth quarter before Hoover connected with Nick Marsh for two touchdowns, including scoring plays covering 75 and 44 yards. Marsh finished with six receptions for 187 yards, giving the Hoosiers another explosive weapon heading into Saturday.

Indiana's success has not depended exclusively on its passing attack. The Hoosiers have developed a balanced offense while maintaining remarkable discipline with the football. Indiana has either won or tied the turnover battle in 30 consecutive games, a streak that highlights the consistency Cignetti has demanded from his players.

That ball security could become particularly important against Ohio State, which features a talented defense coordinated by former NFL head coach Matt Patricia. The Buckeyes will attempt to disguise coverages and pressure Hoover into uncomfortable situations, making his decision-making one of the most important elements of the matchup.
Ohio State's Jeremiah Smith presents enormous challenge for Hoosiers

Indiana's defense has been outstanding this season, but Saturday could provide its most difficult assignment yet. Ohio State wide receiver Jeremiah Smith has established himself as one of college football's most dangerous offensive players, combining size, speed and exceptional playmaking ability.

Smith enters the matchup with more than 900 receiving yards and 11 touchdown catches through six games. He has scored eight touchdowns in his last three contests, demonstrating how quickly he can change the direction of a game. Since the beginning of the 2024 season, Smith has recorded 38 receiving touchdowns, the most of any player in the FBS during that span.

Quarterback Julian Sayin has developed a strong connection with Smith, giving Ohio State an explosive passing attack capable of challenging even the nation's best secondaries. Indiana must find a way to limit those opportunities without allowing the Buckeyes to establish their running game.

The Hoosiers have recorded 20 sacks this season, ranking first in the Big Ten and among the national leaders. Defensive lineman Tobi Osunsanmi has recorded at least one sack in five consecutive games, while Indiana's defense is allowing approximately 75 rushing yards per contest.

Those numbers create a fascinating matchup against Ohio State's offensive line. Indiana sacked Sayin five times during last season's Big Ten Championship Game, and the Hoosiers will attempt to generate similar pressure Saturday. However, Ohio State's receiving talent makes aggressive defensive decisions particularly dangerous if the Buckeyes can exploit one-on-one coverage.
Historic matchup could reshape Big Ten championship race

The atmosphere inside Memorial Stadium should be extraordinary. Indiana has an opportunity to establish another program milestone, while Ohio State is attempting to remind the conference that the Buckeyes remain one of college football's most powerful programs.

Both teams enter with 3-0 Big Ten records, making Saturday's outcome particularly important in the conference championship race. The winner will strengthen its position near the top of the standings while earning a significant victory for its College Football Playoff résumé.

Ohio State has additional motivation after losing last season's conference championship to Indiana. Ryan Day's team also suffered a difficult loss at Texas earlier this season after surrendering a 20-point fourth-quarter advantage, providing another reason for the Buckeyes to emphasize finishing strong against quality opponents.

Indiana, meanwhile, has demonstrated that it can win in several different ways. The Hoosiers have produced explosive offensive performances, relied on defensive pressure and survived close games when circumstances became difficult. Their comeback against Nebraska offered another example of a team that refuses to panic when trailing late.

For Indiana fans, Saturday represents much more than another opportunity to improve to 7-0. It is a chance to watch their program host one of the biggest games in college football, something that once seemed almost unimaginable.

Ohio State has dominated this rivalry historically, but Indiana has changed the conversation. With two top-five teams, national championship implications and a remarkable winning streak on the line, Bloomington will be at the center of the college football world Saturday afternoon.

articles.headline: Russia wants blackout in Ukraine as winter comes — Zelenskyy
keyFacts: Russia attacked more than 15 critical power facilities across Ukraine in an expanded energy campaign, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
Zelenskyy said Russia aims to cause winter blackouts, while US President Donald Trump waived sanctions targeting Russian energy revenues.
Ukrainian services and energy companies are currently conducting restoration work, according to Zelenskyy.
body: Russia is stepping up its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure in a bid to cut electricity and heating in the country as winter approaches, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Saturday.
His remarks come as Moscow intensifies its attacks on civilian targets in the capital, Kyiv, and elsewhere, with key observers saying its objective is to render the country virtually unlivable.
What did Zelenskyy say?

In a post on social media platform X, Zelenskyy said Russia had just carried out one of its biggest attacks on Ukraine's energy sector since it began its full-scale invasion of its neighbor in February 2022.
"More than 15 critical power generation and transmission facilities were targeted across different regions of Ukraine," he wrote.
"Restoration work is ongoing, with all necessary services and all available resources of Ukrainian energy companies involved," he added.
Zelenskyy said that Russia was planning to leave Ukrainian citizens in the cold this winter.

"Russia is trying to cause a blackout in Ukraine — right before winter. Russia is trying to leave millions of our people without electricity and heating," he wrote, calling on allies to put pressure on Moscow to stop this happening.
He said Russia had "expanded its campaign against the energy system" and was trying "to stretch Ukraine's reserves and repair capacity as thinly as possible."
Russia claims multiple infrastructure attacks
The Russian Defense Ministry, for its part, said on Saturday that its forces had attacked several infrastructure targets in Ukraine overnight.
Among those named was an electricity substation in the northwestern city of Zhytomyr.
However, it also said Ukraine's largest steelworks, in the city of Kryvyi Rih, had been hit, saying the facility supplied steel products to the Ukrainian military-industrial complex.
It said another steel plant in Zaporizhzhia, a city near the front line, had also been struck.
Ukrainian authorities have also said that one person — an ambulance driver — was killed and 19 others injured, including a child, in a Russian airstrike on Kherson in southern Ukraine.
Russian state news agency TASS has also reported the death of one woman as a result of Ukrainian drone strikes in Russia's Belgorod region that also injured a man.
Trump's sanctions waiver a boost for Putin: Zelenskyy
Meanwhile, Zelenskyy also reacted to US President Donald Trump's decision to waive a package of new sanctions on Moscow, saying the move would only encourage Russian leader Vladimir Putin.
"A US sanctions blackout, easing pressure on the aggressor, financial rewards for Putin — all of this only encourages him to keep attacking," Zelenskyy said.
On Friday, Trump signed an executive order that waived sweeping US sanctions and tariffs targeting Russia's energy revenues, two days before they were due to take effect.
The waiver has been hailed by a Russian presidential envoy as a "historic moment."
"The Trump administration's suspension of the [Lindsey] Graham Act is an important and truly historic moment," Kirill Dmitriev said on social media.
Dmitriev said the act, named for the late US senator who sponsored the bill, "would have caused "serious damage first and foremost to the US economy and global markets."
Trump's move came as he increasingly criticizes Zelenskyy, fueling speculation that the US leader is siding with Moscow in the conflict.

body: Double Fine's first post-Xbox title, first-person Soulslikes and other new indie games worth checking out
Plus, lots of horror (cozy and otherwise), a colorful platformer and a wolf-battling shepherd dog.

Welcome to our latest roundup of what's going on in the indie game space. As ever, we've got a whole bunch of new games you can jump into this weekend. We'll also dive into some highlights from some of the showcases that aired this week.
The first of those is the Cozy After Dark Showcase. This featured more than 50 games that are eerie, dark, mysterious or otherwise unsettling while just so happening to be a bit cozy as well.

I was happy to see more of a game I'm very excited for, the murder-mystery farming sim Grave Seasons. Developer Perfect Garbage shed extra light on the seasonal farming cycle as well as the game's replayability. The story lasts an in-game year and you can restart it with a new killer and victims while retaining your farming progress.

Other games that stood out to me included DeadRoot (in which you play as a snail that uses a sword and suplexes), Usual June ("a third-person action-adventure game about combat, cupcakes and community") and FallBearers (a co-op game in which you and a friend must overcome obstacles as you transport bodies to their final resting places). Demos for the latter two of those games, others from the showcase and discounts on cozy-but-a-little-scary titles are available through an event on Steam.

The latest Galaxies showcase also featured more than 50 games. Among them were pinball-based top-down shooter Appulse, first-person Western Soulslike Guns of Eschaton and gun-fu/parkour action title Spine, which looks stylish and silly (I'm amped for that one). There were also updates on games including The Finals and Train Sim World 7. There's a Steam event that includes all of the featured games.

If you need even more video game trailers to watch, you may wish to check out The Mix Fall Showcase, which aired on Friday. I haven't had time to watch that yet, unfortunately, but I did see that it included the Saturday morning cartoon-inspired Metroidvania Zozo and the Lost Dreams and puzzle platfomer Nonolith. Both of those look rad and they're firmly on my wishlist.
New indie game releases
Thank You Bus Driver
Developer: Double Fine Productions
Publisher: Double Fine Action Labs
Platforms: Steam (Windows; Steam Deck Verified), Epic Games Store, Itch.io, GOG, Humble Store, Game Jolt
Price: $5

Just a couple of months after departing Xbox, Double Fine has a new game out. Thank You Bus Driver is the first project from Double Fine Action Labs, the studio's label for smaller, experimental games.

In this chaotic riff on Crazy Taxi, you play as a bus driver who yearns for gratitude from unruly passengers. During your journey, your employer will add more rules for you to enforce, such as making sure passengers don't fall asleep or clip their toenails during a ride. You can try to keep them in line with a slap (which reminds me of the delightful Thank Goodness You're Here) or kick them off the bus. All the while, you'll be trying to reach your next stop before the time runs out.
This looks like a fun way to spend a few hours. I can't wait to see what else the newly-independent Double Fine is cooking up.
Valor Mortis
Developer: One More Level
Publishers: Lyrical Games, One More Level
Platforms: Steam (Windows), Xbox Series X/S, PlayStation 5
Price: $40. Available on Game Pass Ultimate and PC Game Pass. The $60 deluxe edition includes an expansion that's set to arrive next year

I really like the Ghostrunner series so I was intrigued when I learned One More Level was moving on to something totally different. Valor Mortis is a first-person Soulslike in which you take on the role of a British soldier who signed up to fight for Napoleon. William was believed to be dead after a battle, but is roused by a corrupted Napoleon (played by Vincent Cassel, of all people). A plague has transformed the other survivors into grotesque enemies, but at least you have supernatural powers at your disposal, along with firearms and melee weapons.

The usual elements of a Soulslike are here. You'll collect catalysts (don't call them souls) from vanquished enemies and spend these on upgrades at checkpoints. Build modifiers are out there in the world for you to find. The developers took some inspiration from Metroidvania games as well, since some new abilities can open up paths and shortcuts.
PS5 and PlayStation Portal owners who'd like to give Valor Mortis a go may want to note that there's a 1.5-hour trial available on PS Plus Premium.
Ratatan
Developers: TVT Co. Ltd., Ratata Arts
Publisher: Game Source Entertainment
Platforms: Steam (Windows; leaving early access), Xbox Series X/S, PS5, Nintendo Switch 2
Price : $35
I've been keeping my eye on this spiritual successor to Patapon from series creator Hiroyuki Kotani for a while. It's a rhythm action game and, because it's 2026, of course it's a roguelite as well.

On each run, you take charge of a group of minions and use rhythm-based commands to tell them what to do. You can launch attacks, reposition your charges to avoid incoming fire and shield them from damage.

I've played a few runs and, even though the framerate is a bit choppy on my PS5, I've enjoyed trying to get to grips with how it all works. The action is more fluid than in traditional turn-based games, but you do have to wait for the music to loop around before you can take any meaningful action. Having to manage that as well as my own character's positioning while accounting for incoming enemy attacks is a lot to juggle. I can't really tell how much impact my elemental attack upgrades are having either.
The artwork is really pretty, though! I'm planning to stick with it a while longer to see if I can figure out how to make more progress.
Colorbound
Developer: Panpipe Studio
Publisher: Whitethorn Games
Platforms: Steam (Windows), Epic Games Store, PS5, Xbox Series X/S, Switch, Switch 2
Price: Usually $15, with a 10 percent discount on Steam until October 26

I like the art style of Colorbound too. This is a platformer in which you use color to reshape the world and solve puzzles. Using a lighter color might make a platform float, and a darker one could make it drop down to where you are.

Panpipe Studio drew from its Chilean culture and heritage for this game, in which you play as Anku, a boy who sets out to reunite his late grandfather's band one last time for a proper sendoff. It looks lovely, and I'm very tempted to pick it up.
Enshrouded
Developer/publisher: Keen Games
Platforms: Steam (Windows; leaving early access), PS5. Coming to Xbox Series X/S in spring 2027
Price: Usually $40, with a 10 percent discount until October 29 (PS Plus required for PS5 discount)

Keen Games gave its co-op survival action RPG Enshrouded a massive update as it brought the game out of early access on Steam. The game also made its debut on PS5 this week. The full map (including a fresh biome) is now open to explore, the story is fully fleshed out — at least for now — and there are higher maximum levels for players and their gear. Keen also overhauled the rendering system as well as the early stages of the game, while adding 14 new enemy types and nine more types of spells.

Perhaps the most interesting update is the new logic system. This creation suite, which is called Sparkworks, lets players craft their own adventures, dungeons and interactive bases that they can share with the community. It sure seems like there's a ton for new and returning players to dig into.
Pixel Washer
Developer: Valadria
Publisher: Acclaim
Platform: Steam (Windows; early access). Coming to Switch 2 in 2027
Price: Usually $13, with a 15 percent discount until October 22

It's still odd to think of Acclaim as an indie publisher, but there's lots about our current reality that doesn't make much sense so I can roll with it. This week, it brought a powerwashing sim (not that one) into the world.

Pixel Washer straps a powerwasher to a piggy. There are no prizes for guessing that your mission is to blast away gunk and grime to make a range of environments look pristine, upgrading your gear as you go.
One of my favorite things about this is that Acclaim looked to the past for the launch trailer. Its narrator is Tim Kitzrow, the voice of NBA Jam (boy, do I hope Acclaim can revive that series).
Penguin Colony
Developer: Origame Digital
Publisher: Fellow Traveller
Platforms: Steam (Windows; Steam Deck Verified), GOG, Humble Store. Coming to Switch and PS5 in 2027
Price: Usually $15, with a 10 percent discount until October 30

It's horror season, so of course we have to highlight a scary game or two. I really love the concept of Penguin Colony. For its follow up to Umurangi Generation, Origame Digital asked, "what if we adapted H.P. Lovecraft's At the Mountains of Madness from the perspective of penguins?"

These birds are just living their lives in the Antarctic in the 1930s when Nazis and Kaitiaki show up in search of an ancient being. I'll leave it to you to determine which group wants to harness the being's destructive power and which would like to make sure it rests for another century. You can swap between different penguins and follow these humans (I'm sure everything will go well for them!) or explore the oddities of this pocket of the world. It'll take multiple playthroughs to discover everything, and I'm intrigued to find out what horrors lie within.
Tenebris Somnia
Developers: Andrés Borghi, Saibot Studios
Publisher: New Blood Interactive
Platforms: Steam (Windows; Steam Deck Verified), Xbox Series X/S, PS5, Switch
Price: $25

I don't think I will ever correctly spell Tenebris Somnia without having to look it up, but this is an interesting game for plenty of other reasons. It's a retro-inspired, pixel-art survival horror game with live-action cutscenes. It's directed by Andrés Borghi, who previously made the gothic fighting game The Black Heart and has worked as a visual effects artist on movies such as When Evil Lurks.

The cutscenes are at the heart of Tenebris Somnia, as they're said to hold the game's secrets. The visuals of those and the gameplay are pulling me in. I wish I had enough time to play all of these neat-looking games!
Hubert
Developer/publisher: Brocap Studio
Platforms: Steam (Windows; demo available). Coming to PS5 later in October
Price: Usually $20, with a 10 percent discount until October 28

Let's wrap things up for this week with a shepherding adventure, because I will always include a dog game if I can. As Hubert, you'll herd sheep through harsh weather and tough terrain with the help of a human. This pup will also need to fend off wolves to keep the flock safe.

It's said to be a short game, lasting about three to four hours. While it's not officially Steam Deck Verified, the developers say Hubert is optimized for Valve's handheld device. I look forward to discovering "poop points" for Hubert on my Deck at some point.

articles.headline: Cybercrims go beyond stealing data to attack physical building systems
keyFacts: Cybercriminals hacked remote-controlled refrigeration systems across hundreds of French grocery stores, spiking temperatures, spoiling food, and sparking fires.
Armis Labs reported that ransomware attackers increasingly use physical disruptions from compromised building automation systems as extortion leverage.
Security experts stated that attackers will increasingly target internet-connected operational technology as organizations improve their information technology defenses.
body: Late Sunday night, a still-unknown cybercriminal or group hacked thousands of remote-controlled refrigeration systems across hundreds of French grocery stores, spiking temperatures, spoiling food, and sparking fires. This is part of an ongoing trend of attacking physical systems that can do damage in the real world.
In August, a ransomware attack disrupted building-management systems at a Canadian hospital, affecting door access controls, central HVAC monitoring, and the issuing of staff access cards.

And three years ago, cyberattacks hit Las Vegas casinos, causing slot machines to go dark, preventing payment kiosks and ATMs from spitting out cash, and locking guests out of their rooms when the electronic keys stopped working.

Not all digital intrusions remain in cyberspace, and attackers don’t need to encrypt files and steal data to cause chaos. Hitting physical systems often produces more severe consequences - and turns up the heat on executives to pay an extortion demand.

“There was one gig where the customer was refusing to pay, and so the threat actor was like, ‘Hold my beer, have fun getting into your offices,’ and locked everybody out,” Tim Beasley, a senior incident response consultant at Semperis, told The Register.
Beasley won’t name the customer, or provide any incriminating information, but said the incident response involved police smashing glass in addition to his team recovering compromised data.

“The cops had to break in, and literally get into the building, breaking some windows, so the customer was able to finally get back in,” he said. We asked if the customer paid the ransom demand, and Beasley yelled: “Oh, hell, no!”

A report published earlier this month by ServiceNow’s Armis Labs found increasing evidence of ransomware attackers using physical consequences as leverage in their intrusions. “Today’s BAS operate at the intersection of IT and OT worlds, creating unprecedented exposure,” the report said.
Ransomware with physical consequences

Building automation systems - BAS - are the critical systems that control and monitor facilities’ HVAC, lighting, energy usage, and water consumption. They also oversee badge readers, door locks, surveillance cameras, fire alarm control panels, and other physical safety equipment.

As such, BAS make very attractive targets for ransomware operators looking for high-pressure ways to extort organizations into paying multi-million ransom demands. These systems also appeal to government-backed goons and hacktivists looking to ensure maximum psychological and physical impact during destructive cyberattacks.

Armis Labs found 73 percent of organizations own BAS that have been used in ransomware attacks, and this same percentage have known exploited vulnerabilities in at least one of their building automation systems. Additionally, 91 percent of BAS communicate over insecure protocols - opening up an even bigger attack surface for cyber-miscreants wanting to cause physical harm.

“The primary thing that we see with any attack on building management systems or physical systems: It’s a great place for the threat actor to hide,” Michael Freeman, ServiceNow’s senior director of threat research, told The Register. “It's easier for them to compromise, and it's easier for them to hide in.”

BAS and operational technology (OT) in general have fewer security controls than IT systems. Most require continual uptime, which makes them harder to patch or even scan for vulnerabilities and misconfigurations as this may lead to outages.

“One case in particular, against a very large financial institution, the threat actors were staying low and quiet by attacking their BMS systems, and then pivoting into the IT environment,” Freeman said.
The intruders were routinely caught - and booted from - the financial institution’s IT systems, so they built backdoors into the BMS to ensure persistent access to both OT and IT networks.
“We're also seeing threat actors using AI to understand more building automation systems, especially ones that are using obscure OSs like VxWorks, older Unix-type systems,” Freeman said.
AI has entered the chat

As multiple security experts have told us in previous interviews, security through obscurity is dead. Not only does AI make it easier for attackers to find bugs – some very obscure and decades old - but it also means criminals no longer need to be OT experts to carry out destructive cyberattacks on critical networks and facilities. Instead, they can use AI to learn all about the obscure protocols and proprietary hardware and software that historically made industrial control systems black boxes.
“It’s easier to understand what the controls are,” Freeman said, using the example of an attacker trying to take down a plane, or some similar catastrophic cyberattack.

Historically, even advanced, government-backed hacking squads would “be quiet, because you don't know what changing certain settings is going to do,” Freeman explained. “Now you can use AI to say, ‘If I compromise a weight and balance system for airlines, all I need to do now is move this number here to this number, and I just told the system to load heavy stuff on the right side of the plane instead of equal distribution.'”

Freeman told us he has seen attackers break into airlines’ OT gear in the past. “But they didn’t know what they were getting into, and so they left them alone,” he said. “Those do cause me concern because in the past I've helped to kick people out of those types of systems.”
Industrial orgs increasingly under attack

OT security provider Dragos tracks ransomware groups’ claims against industrial organizations on the criminals’ leak sites, along with publicly disclosed intrusions affecting manufacturing and other critical sectors. To be clear: claims on leak sites aren’t always accurate or even true, and the claim itself doesn’t mean operations or control systems were hit.
Since 2022, however, “the numbers have been consistently increasing,” Lexie Mooney, senior threat analyst at Dragos, told The Register.
The cybersecurity firm tracked 995 ransomware attacks against industrial orgs in 2023, a 49.5 percent increase from 2022. That number jumped more than 87 percent in 2024.
Active ransomware groups targeting industrial orgs also grew in 2024 to 80 groups, up from 50 the year before.

Dragos tracked 119 ransomware groups impacting more than 3,300 industrial organizations in 2025, and the incidents have steadily increased every quarter this year: 1,020 incidents in the first quarter of 2026 and 1,140 incidents in Q2.

“The vast majority of cases are opportunistic,” Abdul Alamri, a senior threat analyst at Dragos, told us. “In some of the cases that we have seen an operational impact, either physical systems or an OT operation, it’s just the nature of the opportunism on the part of those ransomware groups.”

This is partially due to the complexity of OT systems, he added. “Ransomware groups want to disrupt operations, and put pressure on the victims to pay the ransom,” Alamri said. “They don’t want to invest that time and effort to target complex systems."

It’s usually quicker and easier for financially motivated crims to affect operations via IT systems - as the extortionists did in the August 2025 Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) breach, which halted manufacturing and crippled business operations for months.
Internet-connected OT: the next 'low-hanging fruit'
The other side of this complexity, however, is that many organizations themselves still lack visibility into their OT environments.

Dragos estimates that fewer than 10 percent of OT networks worldwide currently have sufficient network monitoring in place. Plus, in 30 percent of incidents the security firm responded to in 2025, the investigations did not begin with a detection alert, but with someone noticing that “something seemed wrong” in operations.

This lack of visibility, combined with threats from AI, worries Alamri. “If you compare the risk that we have seen from humans, to what we are about to face in the near future with AI agents who might continuously try to break into those systems - it’s a pretty dark future if we don't take the right measures to protect ourselves against it.”

As organizations get better at patching and securing IT systems, attackers will likely look to internet-connected OT systems where digital compromises have real-world consequences, according to Matt Hayden, VP of cyber and emerging threats at General Dynamics Information Technology.
“We all anticipate that as we get better at reducing the IT low-hanging fruit, OT will become a vector of much more scrutiny and much more attention,” Hayden told The Register.
Before joining GDIT, Hayden served as the assistant secretary for cyber, infrastructure, risk and resilience policy at the US Department of Homeland Security.
Compliance vs. security

“There is a big focus on the hardware being connected for the purpose of compliance - and to make sure that, in the name of compliance, we aren't opening back doors, to devices that traditionally wouldn't have to be connected to facilitate their service,” he said, using refrigeration units as an example of one such system that is now internet-connected for compliance purposes.
This was prior to the French supermarket hacks.

Refrigeration units’ monitoring systems connect to the internet so their owners and operators can prove to regulators that the units maintain their uptime and temperature in accordance with regulations.

“So if the health department comes by, they say, ‘Look, my refrigerator was at 27 degrees for the last 72 days,' and they have a check mark, and they get their A plus. But that simple connectivity is also a vector in which that particular refrigerant unit could be targeted for disruption,” Hayden said.
About a week after our interview, criminals did exactly that.

“The recently reported exploitations of commercial refrigeration units represent a significant example of devices without digital value, no sensitive data or extended enterprise access, being exploited by being connected to the internet with unpatched firmware,” Hayden told us in a subsequent email.
He said he expects the attribution to be “less nation-state, and more likely those looking for targets of opportunity to identify what could be done with the unpatched systems.”
“The consequences are food supply degradation at a small scale, but it is an important example of what could happen at scale very quickly with more consequential operating equipment,” Hayden said.®

articles.headline: The Blood of Dawnwalker Update 1.1 adds an easier Story mode, a respec potion and animal petting
keyFacts: Update 1.1 for The Blood of Dawnwalker adds a new easier Story mode, an ability respec potion, and animal petting.
The patch includes camera improvements, uncensored blood in Japan on Steam, and over 1,100 total fixes.
The update is expected to roll out next week.
body: Update 1.1 for The Blood of Dawnwalker will add a new Story mode with additional combat assist, a potion that lets you forget your abilities and master new ones, and the ability to pet dogs and cats.

Expected to roll out next week, the patch also brings changes to combat targeting, the camera and traversal, a FrameGen update, uncensored blood and gore in the Japanese version on Steam, and more than 1,100 other improvements and fixes.
The patch notes were shared on Twitter/X, and they describe several of the changes that game director Konrad Tomaszkiewicz told to our Bertie last month.
The game difficulty formerly known as Story will be rebadged as the 'Forgiving' difficulty, and a different new Story mode, with additional combat assist, will be added.
The Draught of Mind Rebirth will make you forget all your Swordmastery, Witchcraft, and Vampirism abilities, so you can respec and put the time you spent learning them towards a different set.
The update will also, quite rightly, let you pet dogs and cats.
The team is also addressing some technical issues, including an update to the FrameGen technology and dedicated settings.
Here’s what’s coming to The Blood of Dawnwalker with Update 1.1 planned for next week: pic.twitter.com/yi5yaoh3Us
— Dawnwalker (@DawnwalkerGame) October 16, 2026
Here are the patch notes:
New features:

- Draught of Mind Rebirth: Free your mind with the Draught of Mind Rebirth. Forget all your Swordmastery, Witchcraft, and Vampirism abilities, and use the time you spent learning them to master a different set of abilities.
- Petting animals: What happens when you merge a directional combat system with an ability to pet dogs and cats? Directional. Animal. Petting.
- Update to the Story mode: Pick between the Forgiving game difficulty (previously called Story) and a new Story mode with additional combat assist.
- Additional subtitle settings: Increase the font size and enable subtitles for ALL dialogue lines.
Changes and improvements:
- FrameGen update: Update to the FrameGen technology, including dedicated settings.
- Camera improvements: Adjusted animations and camera movements in combat.
- Combat improvements: Improved targeting, locking onto, and disengaging from enemies.
- Traversal improvements: Better responsiveness of targeting and attaching to surfaces when using Shadowstep and Planeshift.
- Japanese version update: Blood and gore will no longer be censored in the Japanese version of the game on Steam.
And over 1,100 other improvements and fixes.
The patch is expected to roll out next week.

The Blood of Dawnwalker arrived in early September and scored four stars on Eurogamer. Bertie praised its novel time-limiting structure and freeform approach, as well as its enjoyable quests and characters, writing: "CD Projekt Red alumni create a familiar dark fantasy adventure, but one with bold and provocative ideas of its own, that's mostly, enormously successful".

articles.headline: Key player in false Talarico rumor has history of online posts invoking Nazi Germany
keyFacts: Influencer Ryan Amacher used a fake name during hospital phone calls to spread false claims that politician James Talarico was hospitalized.
The Guardian reported that Amacher has a long history of online posts praising Nazi Germany and expressing antisemitism and racism.
Amacher canceled an interview after receiving a stand-down order from his attorney amid speculation about potential legal trouble.
body: An influencer who played a key role in hoax claims that James Talarico was in a mental health facility has a long history of social media posts that favorably invoke Nazi Germany, express antisemitism and anti-Black racism, criticize miscegenation and call for “remigration” of refugees.

On X, the Lake Oswego, Oregon, resident Ryan Amacher, known online as Rhein Amacher, has described Muslims as “sub-human”, claimed that Black Africans are “monkeys” with low IQ, characterized immigrants as “vermin” and expressed support for the far right, including Germany’s AfD and the UK’s Tommy Robinson.

His attempt to damage Talarico’s campaign with false claims about a supposed inpatient admission to an Ohio facility fell apart quickly on Sunday night, but not before his claims were boosted by a staffer on the campaign of Talarico’s Republican rival, Ken Paxton. Since working for the Trump campaign in 2024, he has remained in the milieu of Republican politics and rightwing influencers.
Neither Amacher nor the Paxton campaign responded to requests for comment.

Last week, Amacher phoned the Lindner Center of Hope, a psychiatric hospital in Mason, Ohio, three times, trying to confirm a false rumor that Talarico had been admitted there. The rumor apparently began with a 9 October post by an anonymous X account, TickleTexts, which claimed Talarico had been “hospitalized at Lindner Center for HOPE”, and was picked up by the Republican fundraiser Caroline Wren, who falsely tied it to a private flight between Ohio and Austin. Before calling, Amacher had posted as fact that Talarico “was hospitalized at the @LindnerCtrHope” and tagged the hospital asking it to confirm.

In the full recording of the second call, he gives his name as “Tim”, says he wants to send a care package to his cousin, and offers a four-digit patient code. “I simply made one up (2244) in an attempt to bypass the facility’s security restrictions to discuss the patient,” he later wrote on X. For most of the six-minute call the employee tells him she has no record of Talarico. In its final seconds she says a man that looks like Talarico “was just discharged this evening”.

An excerpt of the recording was incorporated into a 47-second clip that Nick Sortor posted on Sunday afternoon under the headline “Ohio mental hospital CONFIRMS James Talarico was discharged from the facility earlier this week”. Amacher posted his own version minutes later, and Elon Musk replied with a characteristic “!!”. Amacher had first offered the recording to Blaze Media and the Daily Mail, which reportedly declined to run it, and said in an X Space that evening that influencers are “not held to the same journalistic standards”. By Tuesday he had reportedly pulled out of an interview with the writer and podcaster Jesse Singal, saying his attorney had given him a “stand down order”.
The purported legal advice coincides with coverage of the fiasco, which has included speculation that Amacher’s attempt to access private health information may land him in legal trouble.
Previous coverage, however, has not probed Amacher’s long history of extremist commentary.
‘Modern Freikorps volunteers are needed’
Amacher often invokes Nazi Germany, and the paramilitary movement that preceded it, with apparent admiration.

“In 1919, Germany’s defeated soldiers came home only to be stabbed in the back by socialists and communists who wanted to burn the nation down and install a Soviet-style dictatorship,” he wrote on 29 July, over an AI-generated image of German soldiers beneath Soviet flags beside uniformed men under crescent moons at Berlin’s Brandenburg Gate. In a follow-up post he wrote: “Modern Freikorps volunteers are needed to step up to purge the German nation of the filth destroying it from within.” An AI-generated image accompanying it showed a masked soldier wearing “Freikorps” and “Deutsches Reich” patches, with the black, white and red flag of imperial Germany flying over the Reichstag.

The Freikorps were paramilitary units of demobilized soldiers that crushed leftwing uprisings in Germany after the first world war. In January 1919, Freikorps troops murdered the communist leaders Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht. In June, Amacher told critics to “read up on the German Freikorps after 1919–and what became of Luxemburg and Liebknecht”.

“History has a way of repeating itself when revolutionary movements collide with a nation pushed to the brink,” he added. The Freikorps are widely seen as an ideological ancestor of Adolf Hitler’s Nazi party, though he later turned against them.

In July, replying to a post that said “we fought the wrong enemy in WW2, just like General Patton said before the jews assassinated him in 1945”, Amacher wrote: “We should have immediately re-armed the German Wehrmacht and auxiliary troops and joined forces to defeat Soviet communism, once and for all!”
Patton died in December 1945 after a car crash in occupied Germany; conspiratorial claims that he was assassinated have long been debunked.

When fellow influencer Cam Higby complained in February that saying Nick Shirley was not a Nazi had led others to call him one, Amacher replied that “a colleague’s great-grandfather served as a paramilitary adjunct in Germany’s ‘other’ military force (not the Wehrmacht)”. He went on: “By your logic, does that make him a Nazi? Asking for a friend…” and attaching an “OK” emoji.

He has captioned a photo of a figure skater with her right arm raised “Heil yes!” and offered to recruit a man “straight into my elite Panzer division”. Panzer divisions were armored tank units in Nazi Germany’s army. In July 2025 he joked that his ancestors “fled to Argentina as well, but way back in 1945, departing from the Deutsches Reich”.

He has also called for the return of the late Spanish dictator Francisco Franco, writing: “Bring back Francisco Franco!” in July under a post claiming that “African military-aged males by the THOUSANDS” were entering the Spanish enclave of Ceuta. And he has praised Germany’s AfD, which the country’s domestic intelligence agency labeled a “confirmed rightwing extremist” force last year. “The @AfD is the ONLY party left that will actually SAVE Germany from destruction,” he wrote in April. “We will restore traditional German societal norms, identity, and culture.”
‘He looks like a Jew’
In January, replying to a post attacking the San Francisco Democrat Scott Wiener, Amacher wrote: “He looks like a Jew–I’m guessing he is a Jew!,” and included a nose emoji.

In May 2025, after another user wrote of a man that “He’s also jewish, no surprise there”, Amacher replied: “A ginger Jew? Worst of both worlds…” Under a December post blaming Somali Muslims in Minnesota for “the largest theft of tax payer dollars in American History”, he wrote: “Both peoples are despicable, but the Somalis are ahead of the Jews by far!”

He has told a pro-Israel account that it was “a hollowed-out puppet dancing on Zionist strings” whose loyalty was “to a parasitic regime halfway across the world”, and written that “Zionist infiltrators have sunk their claws deep into U.S. policy”.

Another recurring subject is George Soros, the Jewish financier who is a frequent target of antisemitic conspiracy theories. Amacher has called him “a spawn of the Devil himself”, and in February 2025 wrote that Soros “allegedly turned in his own people during WWII just to save his own skin”, a claim factcheckers have repeatedly debunked.
‘Monkeys typically have an estimated IQ below 70’

In June, TickleTexts, the anonymous account that started the Talarico rumor, baselessly claimed, “as a born South African”, that “some villages believe r*ping a 6 month old baby girl will cure their AIDS”. Amacher replied: “Monkeys typically have an estimated IQ below 70.”

Replying in January to a post about a Somali asylum seeker who, it claimed, had raped a 10-year-old girl in Denmark, he wrote: “Seriously, f*ck international obligations! These people are sub-human animals meant for zoos for viewing purposes only!” In February, he wrote that a dog said to have led police in Louisville, Kentucky, to a missing three-year-old had “demonstrated an intelligence far superior to that of any illegal Somali invader!”

In June, he credited Nick Shirley, whose videos about Somali-run daycare centers in Minnesota set off a national panic, with exposing a “mastermind” who, Amacher wrote, had “funded the savage, low-IQ black Tusken Raiders fleecing Minnesota taxpayers”. In January, under a post about Trump’s claim that fraud in Minnesota could reach $80bn, he proposed “one-way, remigration flights back to Somalia as starters!”
‘Future super predators in the making’

In June 2025, after another user told the Hodgetwins, a pair of Black conservative YouTubers, that they were “NO longer welcome”, Amacher wrote: “I’m waiting for their response of, ‘hey sorry, blame it on my negro brain!’”

On 7 October he replied to a comment about “the white girl in the front” of an image: “Getting strong mudshark vibes with that one.” “Mudshark” is a racist slur for a white woman who partners with Black men.

Last November, under a post about “a mob of black ‘kids’” accused of attacking a pregnant woman in Chicago, he wrote: “F*cking savages and future super predators in the making!” In May, replying to a post about a weekend of shootings in Chicago, he wrote: “You can’t override biology or selectively breed out the ‘predator’ gene in certain populations.”

In June, under a post claiming that “the biggest scandal in American history” was “convincing millions of people that Michelle Obama is beautiful”, Amacher wrote: “Hey now–‘BIG Mike’ ain’t playing around! No monkey business here…” The reference to “Big Mike” probably comes from a baseless conspiracy theory that Michelle Obama is a man.

That month, Karmelo Anthony was convicted of murder in Texas for the 2025 stabbing of a fellow student, 17-year-old Austin Metcalf. Replying to a video of a crowd of Anthony’s supporters, most of them Black, outside the trial, Amacher wrote: “I hope none of these animals breed.”
‘Remigration is the ONLY answer’

Since November 2025, Amacher has used the word “remigration” in more than 30 posts. The term, promoted by Europe’s far right, describes the mass deportation of migrants; plans discussed at a meeting in Potsdam attended by AfD members included people with German citizenship. Last month Germany’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, accused the AfD of pursuing an “ethnic cleansing” policy.

“The word for 2026 is remigration!” Amacher posted in January. Asked by another user in November 2025 what should happen to Muslims in America, he replied: “Remigration to native homelands for those with insufficient loyalties.” In April he shared an AfD video with the comment: “Remigration is the ONLY answer–great video by the @AfD!”

In June, under a post complaining about the Muslim call to prayer in Dearborn, Michigan, he wrote: “These sub-humans must be forcibly extracted from America and shipped off in crates back to the Middle East.”

He has also cheered Jake Lang, a pardoned January 6 rioter who has led anti-Muslim protests. Replying last November to a post about clashes between Muslim residents and Christian protesters in Dearborn, where rightwing influencers have staged anti-Islam rallies, Amacher wrote: “Jake is the general leading our generation’s Crusade to save our nation’s cultural identity and heritage. Brave, fearsome, and ready to drive out the foreign invaders!” When Lang led a protest in Plano, Texas, in December “against the Islamic takeover of America”, Amacher tagged him in a post calling him “the leader for the next Crusades!” On 21 December he wrote that he had texted Lang to confirm he was “not Jewish”. Earlier this month, he posted: “We need another Crusades–except on our own home turf!”

Two national guard members were shot in Washington DC last November, and an Afghan man, Rahmanullah Lakanwal, was arrested as the suspect. That evening Amacher wrote that the attacker “should be publicly executed in Lafayette Square using bacon grease, with the entire nation watching”. He added: “This will send a clear message to third world invaders that we will not tolerate their presence!”

Other posts urge that migrants be shot, or rounded up by ordinary citizens. Under a June 2025 post by the British far-right activist Tommy Robinson about a defaced statue of Joan of Arc in Paris, he wrote: “These invaders don’t deserve deportation–better yet, shoot them and save the cost!” This June he wrote that “those uncivilized savages can leave Britain on their own–or be removed at gunpoint by a mob of furious native Britons”.

Replying in April to Nick Sortor’s post that “hard choices are going to have to be made soon”, he wrote that if the federal government would not deport “these third-world invaders, then we, the American people, will have no choice but to hunt them down ourselves, round them up like the illegal trash they are, and throw their asses back across the border where they belong!”

“Bounty hunters get paid to track down bail jumpers and hand them over,” he wrote in July. “We should be able to do the exact same thing with illegal immigrants–hunt them down, turn them in to @ICEgov, and get rewarded.”

Public records show Amacher has used two first names. Oregon business filings list Ryan David Amacher, at a house in Lake Oswego, as the registered agent of Amacher & Company LLC, formed in 2012. In 2018, a letter from “Ryan Amacher” calling for the repeal of US immigration law drew a rebuttal in the Lake Oswego Review. By 2024 he was signing himself Rhein: federal campaign finance records list “Rhein Amacher”, at the same address, as the company’s president, and his columns in the Review now carry that name. Last year a Portland police dispatcher logged a call from “RYAN AMACHER” at the city’s ICE facility, while officers ran a records check on “Rhein David” Amacher. The Daily Mail has reported that his “real name is Ryan”.

Until now, Amacher has been a lower-tier player in a rightwing influencer economy whose currency includes live streams of contentious events, tendentious coverage of perceived political foes, and disinformation campaigns.

Even now, his social media following is relatively modest. His biggest platform is X, where his follower count (about 35,000) is dwarfed by those of similar rightwing creators such as Nick Shirley (1.8m), Nick Sortor (1.6m) and Katie Daviscourt (512,000).

His first brushes with broader notoriety came during anti-ICE protests in his native Portland, Oregon, last year, when his antagonism toward protesters extended to the self-confessed theft of leaf blowers and other items from an abandoned protest camp.

articles.headline: Ilhan Omar's turbulent week explained: The dueling probes that threw the Somali-born progressive into chaos
keyFacts: Federal agents raided Representative Ilhan Omar's home as part of an investigation into whether she or her father committed immigration fraud.
U.S. Attorney Jeannine Pirro separately announced an investigation into discrepancies found in Omar's congressional financial disclosures.
Omar called the raid a politically motivated abuse of power, while administration officials stated that investigators will follow the law.
body: It was a week of legal turmoil for one of America's most recognizable members of Congress.

Early Monday morning, federal agents with Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), the chief investigative arm of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), executed a search warrant on Washington, D.C. home of Rep. Ilhan Omar , D-Minn.

The raid was part of an ongoing criminal probe into Omar's immigration status, with sources telling Fox News Digital that authorities are scrutinizing whether she or her father committed fraud when filling out paperwork for her to become a U.S. citizen.

A day later, U.S. Attorney for the District of Washington, D.C., Jeannine Pirro, announced her office was investigating Omar's financial disclosures , which had previously been subject to public scrutiny and congressional oversight, but never by authorities.
FEDERAL AGENTS RAID ILHAN OMAR’S DC HOME AMID IMMIGRATION FRAUD INVESTIGATION
Fox News Digital breaks down what we know so far about each investigation:

In May 2025, Omar filed financial disclosure forms for the year 2024, a required for every member of Congress to complete every year. I showed that she had between $6 million and $30 million in assets connected to two businesses run by her husband, Tim Mynett. One was was a venture capital firm, and the other a California winery.
Her financial disclosures from the year prior, covering 2023, said those assets were only valued at between $15,000 and $51,000 total.

The now-defunct winery, eStCru LLC, saw its reported valuation jump from between $15,000 and $50,000 in 2023 to between $1 million and $5 million in 2024. Rose Lake Capital LLC showed an even sharper increase, rising from a reported value of between $1 and $1,000 in 2023 to between $5 million and $25 million the following year.

The massive reported spike in net worth over the one-year span raised eyebrows, leading a watchdog group called the National Legal and Policy Center to file a complaint with the Office of Congressional Conduct in February of this year.
'SQUAD' DEM DISMISSES FRAUD PROBE SPECULATION AFTER $29M NET-WORTH DROP

Less than a month after the complaint was filed, Omar amended her 2025 disclosure form. The new filing reduced the couple's combined reported assets to between $18,004 and $95,000, and said the businesses had zero value after accounting for liabilities.
ILHAN OMAR'S OFFICE SAYS SHE'S ‘NOT A MILLIONAIRE’ AFTER $30M FILING REVISED DOWN TO UNDER $100K: REPORT
Omar blamed an accounting error, and has since repeatedly insisted that she is not a millionaire.
In September, the Office of Congressional Conduct voted 5-1 to recommend that the House Ethics Committee dismiss misconduct allegations stemming from the financial disclosures.
But the hubbub caught the eye of Pirro, who confirmed on Fox News' "America Reports" Tuesday that her office is investigating the discrepancies.
Further details about the investigation have not yet been released.

Monday's judicially authorized raid of Omar's Washington, D.C. home sent shockwaves through the political world, with many critics calling it politically motivated because it occurred three weeks before November's general elections.
The Trump administration has denied those accusations.
DEMOCRATS' FURY OVER ILHAN OMAR RAID DRAWS STINGING GOP REMINDER ABOUT RAID FROM THE PAST: ‘SET THE PRECEDENT’

HSI agents spent several hours at Omar's home, and the Wall Street Journal reported that the lawmaker's personal cell phone, computers and passport were seized during the search. She has not been seen publicly since before the raid.

Sources told Fox News Digital that investigators are scrutinizing whether Omar or her father fraudulently filled out immigration paperwork when Omar was become a U.S. citizen decades ago. The Journal also reported that the goal of the probe is to strip Omar of her citizenship.
A dozen people, including family members, were subpoenaed in relation to the investigation.
FEDERAL AGENTS SEIZE PHONE OF REP ILHAN OMAR IN RAID TIED TO IMMIGRATION FRAUD PROBE

"Well, I understand they’re looking at her very carefully," President Donald Trump said Monday of the raid. "I’ve always found her to be totally crooked, personally, but that has nothing to do with me."

"I think she’s a terrible person. Just a complainer. She comes from a country that is ... a non-country, and then she comes over here and she complains about our Constitution," he continued. "I think she’s a terrible person, but that’s really up to the DOJ. I have nothing to do with it."
On Tuesday in an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital after rallying for Republican U.S. Senate candidate Ken Paxton in Tyler, Texas, Vice President JD Vance echoed a similar sentiment.

"We don't want to be like the Biden administration. We never want to be like that — where they would allow the law to go after their political opponents," Vance said. "We really want to let the law, the facts drive this. And if justice requires something else be done, then, of course, we'll take a step when we have to."
ILHAN OMAR’S EMBATTLED HUSBAND APPEARS AT SCENE OF HSI RAID IN MIDST OF CRIMINAL FRAUD INVESTIGATION
Vance made it clear taking that unprecedented step of denaturalizing a sitting member of Congress is possible, but only if the law requires it based on the facts of the case.
"And to the question of it being unprecedented, I mean, what I'd say is that Ilhan Omar herself is a very unprecedented person," Vance said.
"We have very rarely had a person in Congress who seems to have such disdain and such rage at the country that gave her a better life," Vance said. "Now, that's not a crime."
"But we're going to see whether she did commit a crime. And if she did, we're obviously going to follow the law."
A spokesperson for Omar did not return multiple requests for comment throughout the week.
However, Omar has responded on social media.
"This raid by Trump’s DHS is an outrageous abuse of power and an unprecedented escalation in the weaponization of federal law enforcement to target political enemies," she said.

"For a decade, Donald Trump has relentlessly targeted Congresswoman Ilhan Omar with inflammatory rhetoric, repeatedly putting a target on her back. Now, those attacks have escalated to a pointless federal raid. The Congresswoman has done nothing wrong. No president should be able to use the power of the federal government to intimidate his political enemies."

articles.headline: Decades after apartheid, South Africans seek justice for crimes of the past
keyFacts: Sharpeville survivors and victims' families filed a court challenge against an apartheid-era law to seek reparations through a class-action lawsuit.
The lawsuit is part of a wider legal movement seeking accountability and reparations for apartheid-era crimes in South Africa.
If the court finds the law unconstitutional and certifies the class action, individual damages claims could follow for victims' families.
body: Decades after apartheid, South Africans seek justice for crimes of the past
SHARPEVILLE, South Africa – Paulina Mathinye gestures with anguish at the rows of garbage-strewn graves, overrun with weeds, in the cemetery where her father is buried.

"Look at that, where they sleep," she says of the dozens of Black protesters buried here, all of whom were killed when police opened fire on March 21, 1960 in what became one of the bloodiest days in apartheid history.
"Why are they dirty? It's a disgrace," says the 71-year-old grandmother, who wears a floral dress and a smart sunhat.

The cemetery, like much else in this visibly poor township about an hour's drive from Johannesburg, has been left to decay. But Mathinye notes that for one day a year at least, when South Africa's political elite descend to commemorate the massacre, the graveyard is spotless. The anniversary is a public holiday known as Human Rights Day.
"I'm still angry. My anger comes out because that's the day my father was shot," says Mathinye, who was just five years old at the time.
She says her father's part in what became a turning point in the struggle against apartheid has not been sufficiently recognized by the current democratic government.
And she says she wants justice – however delayed.
That's why she's signed up to take part in a potential class action lawsuit 66 years later, along with Sharpeville survivors and the families of Sharpeville victims.
At least 69 people were shot by police that day. They had been demonstrating against the country's pass laws – which restricted black people's movements and where they could live and work.
While it's unclear if any perpetrators are still alive, those taking part in the case hope it could lead to reparations.

But first, the group's lawyers must challenge an apartheid-era law that continues to block their efforts to seek legal redress. The law remains in force decades after apartheid ended and a Black-majority government took power.

In September they filed an application in the Gauteng High Court challenging the continued existence of the Indemnity Act 61 of 1961. If the court finds the law unconstitutional, and also certifies a class action for survivors and dependants of those killed, then claims for individual damages could follow.
Mathinye says the repercussions of that day in 1960 have affected her whole life.
Without her father, the main breadwinner, she couldn't finish school. That, in turn, affected the lives of her children and grandchildren.
"So we struggled a lot. And we are still struggling now, because nothing has been happening," she told NPR.
If the case goes ahead and succeeds, Paulina says she'll use any money from reparations to fix up her modest home and pay for her four grandkids' educations.
Part of a wider trend
The Sharpeville case is just one in a new wave of legal efforts that are seeking truth, accountability and reparations for apartheid-era crimes before it's too late.

"It's crucial that these issues of deep injustice are properly dealt with and that South Africa confronts them and does not sweep them under the carpet," says Daniel Leader, an international human rights lawyer advising the South African legal team representing the Sharpeville survivors and families.
Other cases include a court ruling last year that found South Africa's first Nobel Peace Prize laureate, Chief Albert Luthuli, was beaten to death by apartheid police in 1967.

Luthuli, the former leader of the African National Congress — Nelson Mandela's party — had previously been ruled to have died after being struck by a train. The new ruling overturned the finding of an earlier inquest.

The inquest into the 1985 killings of four anti-apartheid activists known as the "Cradock Four" has also been reopened. The activists were abducted and killed by apartheid security forces near the Eastern Cape town of Cradock. Although the officers involved are all dead, the victims families hope the inquest will establish who ordered the killings.
And the inquest into the torture and death of Steve Biko, the iconic Black Consciousness leader who died in police detention in 1977, has also returned to court.

"It's very clear that the murder of Steve Biko was exactly that, murder," Biko's son Nkosinathi told media in September at the reopened inquest. "We hope that this inquest will eventually get to this very certain, unambiguous finding."
The original inquest in 1977 heard from members of the security branch who said Biko had fallen and hit his head in a "scuffle with security police."

The Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC), a court-like restorative justice body set up in the 1990s to uncover the truth about human rights violations during apartheid, re-examined the Biko case.
It denied amnesty to security officers who testified, saying they hadn't been truthful. That essentially cleared the way for possible prosecutions, but they never happened.

In fact, hundreds of the TRC's recommendations for prosecutions were delayed or never pursued. Last year, President Cyril Ramaphosa established a formal inquiry to investigate whether the recommendations were deliberately shelved.

The inquiry is looking into whether there was a secret deal between the old leaders of the apartheid regime and the country's new Black leaders not to prosecute cases in the interests of reconciliation. Its findings are due in December.
Back at the Sharpeville cemetery, Paulina Mathinye and three other descendants of those killed in the massacre, pause in front of a memorial plaque before exiting the graveyard.
Vincent Thamae, from the NGO, Voices of Sharpeville which works with survivors and descendants asks that they take leave of the dead.
"We ask of those who are sleeping here to be with us as we pursue justice for them," he says.
